sections.title: What RazorCAD is
sections.text: RazorCAD is a parametric part modeller for Windows with a classic feature-tree interface. You build a part as a feature history: sketches, extrudes, revolves, cuts, fillets, patterns and so on, each of which can be edited later. Changing a dimension or an equation rebuilds every feature after it. Solid modelling runs on the OpenCascade B-rep kernel (the engine behind FreeCAD), through the replicad library. Display uses three.js. RazorCAD runs fully offline. Main capabilities: Constraint-driven 2D sketches with relations, dimensions and equations, plus gear and airfoil generators 3D sketches for frames, pipe and duct routes and sweep paths Solid features: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, hole, helix, threads, wrap, draft, rib, dome, patterns, mirror, fillet, chamfer, shell Multi-body parts with combine, subtract, split, move/copy, per-body materials and appearances Surface modelling: extruded, revolved, planar, lofted, swept, filled, boundary and ruled surfaces, trim, extend, knit, thicken and more Sheet metal: flanges, hems, miter flanges, sketched bends, jogs, forming tools, tab and slot, lofted bends, transitions, flat patterns and DXF export Fast Structure (weldments): structural members from standard profiles, end caps, gussets, weld beads and a cut list Assemblies with mates (including gear and rack-pinion mates), sub-assemblies, configurations, standard parts and fastener sets, equations shared with the parts, holes and cuts made in the assembly, exploded views, motion studies, collision detection, an interference check, a bill of materials with mass and cost, and STEP export 2D drawings of parts and assemblies, with projected, section, detail, auxiliary, broken, exploded and flat pattern views, dimensions (also made automatically), GD&T, cosmetic threads, balloons, bill-of-materials tables, a drawing check, DXF drawings placed on the sheet, and PDF and DXF export Millimetres or inches, chosen for each document STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ and 3MF import; STEP, STL, OBJ, 3MF and glTF export; DXF import into sketches and drawings, and DXF export of faces and flat patterns Macros, recorded or written, that drive RazorCAD English, German, French or Spanish, a light or dark theme, and keyboard use of the panels An Ask Claude panel that builds features from a plain-language description A browser version at razorcad.com/app, the same program without installing anything
sections.html:
RazorCAD is a parametric part modeller for Windows with a classic feature-tree interface. You build a part as a feature history: sketches, extrudes, revolves, cuts, fillets, patterns and so on, each of which can be edited later. Changing a dimension or an equation rebuilds every feature after it.

Solid modelling runs on the OpenCascade B-rep kernel (the engine behind FreeCAD), through the replicad library. Display uses three.js. RazorCAD runs fully offline.

Main capabilities:

  • Constraint-driven 2D sketches with relations, dimensions and equations, plus gear and airfoil generators
  • 3D sketches for frames, pipe and duct routes and sweep paths
  • Solid features: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, hole, helix, threads, wrap, draft, rib, dome, patterns, mirror, fillet, chamfer, shell
  • Multi-body parts with combine, subtract, split, move/copy, per-body materials and appearances
  • Surface modelling: extruded, revolved, planar, lofted, swept, filled, boundary and ruled surfaces, trim, extend, knit, thicken and more
  • Sheet metal: flanges, hems, miter flanges, sketched bends, jogs, forming tools, tab and slot, lofted bends, transitions, flat patterns and DXF export
  • Fast Structure (weldments): structural members from standard profiles, end caps, gussets, weld beads and a cut list
  • Assemblies with mates (including gear and rack-pinion mates), sub-assemblies, configurations, standard parts and fastener sets, equations shared with the parts, holes and cuts made in the assembly, exploded views, motion studies, collision detection, an interference check, a bill of materials with mass and cost, and STEP export
  • 2D drawings of parts and assemblies, with projected, section, detail, auxiliary, broken, exploded and flat pattern views, dimensions (also made automatically), GD&T, cosmetic threads, balloons, bill-of-materials tables, a drawing check, DXF drawings placed on the sheet, and PDF and DXF export
  • Millimetres or inches, chosen for each document
  • STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ and 3MF import; STEP, STL, OBJ, 3MF and glTF export; DXF import into sketches and drawings, and DXF export of faces and flat patterns
  • Macros, recorded or written, that drive RazorCAD
  • English, German, French or Spanish, a light or dark theme, and keyboard use of the panels
  • An Ask Claude panel that builds features from a plain-language description
  • A browser version at razorcad.com/app, the same program without installing anything

sections.title: Running RazorCAD
sections.text: Double-click RazorCAD.exe. It is one standalone program: it needs no browser, Python or installation, and it runs offline. It uses the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime, which comes with Windows 10 and 11.
sections.html: Double-click RazorCAD.exe. It is one standalone program: it needs no browser, Python or installation, and it runs offline. It uses the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime, which comes with Windows 10 and 11.

sections.title: RazorCAD in your browser
sections.text: razorcad.com/app runs the same RazorCAD in a web browser (Microsoft Edge, Chrome and other current browsers), with nothing to install: parts, sketches, assemblies, drawings and macros, on the same geometry kernel. Open reads a file from your PC and Save downloads it. Preferences stay in that browser. There is no auto-save, no Windows fonts (the fonts that come with RazorCAD are used) and no Ask Claude sign-in. A notice at the top says so and links to the Windows app; ✕ closes it for good. Parts that take a while to build are kept in the browser's own storage (up to 400 MB), so they open quickly the next time. Closing the browser tab with unsaved work asks first.

sections.title: Installing with the setup program
sections.text: Testers can be given RazorCAD-Setup.exe, a single setup program with RazorCAD inside it. Install for the current user (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\RazorCAD, no administrator rights), for all users (Program Files), or into a folder you choose. Setup installs the Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime and .NET Framework 4.8 from Microsoft if they are missing. It creates Start-menu and desktop shortcuts and registers RazorCAD under Windows Installed apps with an uninstaller. The uninstaller asks before removing settings and crash reports. Part files are never touched. Running setup again updates an existing installation. Until RazorCAD is code-signed, Windows may show "Windows protected your PC" for the setup: click More info, then Run anyway. The Read me first file that comes with the setup says what to expect for that version. Silent install and uninstall: Command Effect --- --- RazorCAD-Setup.exe /S Silent install for the current user /D=folder Install into this folder /ALLUSERS Install for all users /NODESKTOP, /NOSTARTMENU Skip the desktop or Start-menu shortcut uninstall.exe /S Silent uninstall

sections.title: Updates
sections.text: A little after it starts (at most once a day), RazorCAD asks GitHub for the newest RazorCAD release. When there is a newer one, a notice in the corner offers Download (the release page), Later or Skip this version. Nothing is shown when you are up to date or offline. Only GitHub is asked; nothing about you or your parts is sent. Help ▸ Check for Updates… checks at once and says what it found. Its window also turns the check at start on or off. Help ▸ About RazorCAD shows the version you have. Update Now (in the notice and in Check for Updates) updates in one click: RazorCAD downloads the new setup from its GitHub release, checks it against the release (size and SHA-256), installs it into the same folder (asking for administrator rights only when it was installed for all users), closes and starts again as the new version. Unsaved work is saved first (Save All and Update), or the update waits. The helper waits for this installation's app and launcher processes to close, checks the installer result, verifies that the executable was replaced and that the installed version matches the download, then restarts. A failed installation shows an error and its log path instead of silently reopening the old version. A copy of RazorCAD that wasn't installed with the setup offers Download instead. If updating fails, inspect %TEMP%\RazorCAD-update\update.log and run the downloaded setup in that folder manually after closing RazorCAD. The helper script is saved beside it as install-update.ps1. Fixes to the updater itself take effect once a build containing them has been installed; an older installation may need the newer setup run manually once.

sections.title: The start window
sections.text: At launch RazorCAD shows a start window with: New to RazorCAD? Take the one-minute tour (until you have taken it; see Getting Started Tour) New Part, New Assembly and New Drawing Open… Sample Part, a ready-made part to explore Recent Parts: name, folder and date. Missing files are greyed out and can be removed with ✕. Parts that have an auto-save waiting are marked. Recover Previous Session, offered once when unsaved work from an earlier version is found A notice when new crash reports have been written Reopen it any time with File ▸ Recent Parts / Start….
sections.html:
At launch RazorCAD shows a start window with:

  • New to RazorCAD? Take the one-minute tour (until you have taken it; see Getting Started Tour)
  • New Part, New Assembly and New Drawing
  • Open…
  • Sample Part, a ready-made part to explore
  • Recent Parts: name, folder and date. Missing files are greyed out and can be removed with ✕. Parts that have an auto-save waiting are marked.
  • Recover Previous Session, offered once when unsaved work from an earlier version is found

Reopen it any time with File ▸ Recent Parts / Start….

sections.title: The RazorCAD window
sections.text: Area What it does --- --- Menu bar File, Edit, View, Insert, Tools, Help. Next to the menus are quick buttons for Save, Save As, Rebuild and Search commands (the magnifier). Document tabs Each open part or drawing has its own tab. ✕ closes a tab and asks to save. Command ribbon Tabs of tool buttons: Features, Sketch, Surfaces, Sheet Metal, Fast Structure, Evaluate and Claude. Buttons with a shortcut show the key in their bottom-right corner. Feature tree The part's history, with folders for Solid Bodies, Sheet Metal Bodies and Surface Bodies, the material, the planes and every feature. An eye column on the right shows or hides each item. Configurations tab Next to the Feature tree and the Property panel at the top of the left panel (see the Configurations chapter) Property panel Opens in place of the tree while you create or edit a feature. ✔ accepts (Enter), ✕ cancels (Esc). Heads-up toolbar Above the 3D view: view orientation, display style, selection filters, visibility (eye button) and section view Confirm corner The top-right corner of the view holds ✔ / ✕ for the active feature or sketch Status line and progress bar Bottom left. Long operations (opening, rebuilding, importing, meshing, exporting) show progress here. The rebuild time is shown at the right; when features have errors it shows their number in red: click it for Fix References. Units Bottom right: MMGS (millimetres) or IPS (inches). Click it to change the document's units.

sections.title: Customising the ribbon
sections.text: The ribbon shows its buttons in two rows. Icon size: Small, Medium or Large, from View ▸ Toolbar Icons or by right-clicking the ribbon. Rearrange: drag a button to a new place; the others slide aside. Your own toolbars: click + after the tabs (or right-click a tab ▸ New Toolbar…). Add tools by dragging a button onto its tab or with right-click ▸ Add to "…". Drag a button off to remove it. Right-click a button on a built-in toolbar to hide it or add a separator after it. Customize Toolbars… shows hidden buttons again, and Reset puts a toolbar back as it was. In Customize Toolbars…, choose Sketch and set Sketch toolbar layout to Expanded (all tools) or Grouped (flyout menus). Grouped mode gathers lines, rectangles, arcs, splines and slots under split buttons. Click the main icon to start the last-used variant; click the adjacent arrow to choose another variant. The icon and label follow the saved choice. With a family tool active, its Type selector in the Property panel offers the same variants, in both toolbar layouts. Choices made with shortcuts or individual toolbar buttons are remembered too. Each family remembers its own variant between sessions. The layout preference is saved, and changing it preserves the expanded toolbar order and hidden tools. Use Expanded mode to rearrange individual tools. The layout is kept in prefs.json in RazorCAD's data folder.

sections.title: Settings
sections.text: File ▸ Settings… or Tools ▸ Settings… (in parts, assemblies and drawings) has everything you can set in one place; a change applies at once: Appearance: theme, language, the size of the toolbar icons, and the Sketch toolbar's layout (all tools, or grouped in flyout menus). Units and Axes: the units of the part, assembly or drawing shown, and its up axis (also used for new parts). Sheet Metal Gauges: the gauges you saved (from a sheet metal feature's Gauge row, Save…); delete the ones you no longer want. More Settings: DXF Settings, Customize Shortcuts, Customize Toolbars, Claude Settings and the Getting Started Tour.
sections.html:
File ▸ Settings… or Tools ▸ Settings… (in parts, assemblies and drawings) has everything you can set in one place; a change applies at once:

  • Appearance: theme, language, the size of the toolbar icons, and the Sketch toolbar's layout (all tools, or grouped in flyout menus).
  • Units and Axes: the units of the part, assembly or drawing shown, and its up axis (also used for new parts).
  • Sheet Metal Gauges: the gauges you saved (from a sheet metal feature's Gauge row, Save…); delete the ones you no longer want.
  • More Settings: DXF Settings, Customize Shortcuts, Customize Toolbars, Claude Settings and the Getting Started Tour.

sections.title: Language and theme
sections.text: View ▸ Language: English, Deutsch, Français or Español, in parts, assemblies and drawings. The menus, ribbons, Property panels, dialog titles and buttons, the tree's fixed items and the start window are translated; longer help texts and messages are still in English. The command search finds a command by its translated name or its English one. Macros, recordings and your shortcuts work in every language, and files are the same in all of them. View ▸ Theme: Light, Dark, or Follow Windows (switches when Windows does). In the dark theme the window, the 3D view and sketches are dark; drawing sheets stay white paper. Both are kept with your preferences.

sections.title: Getting Started Tour
sections.text: A one-minute tour of the window in eight short steps, each pointing at its part of the window: the ribbon, the feature tree, the view and its mouse buttons, how to make a first part, the command search and the units. It ends with Open the Sample Part. Use Next / Back (or → / ← and Enter); Esc or Skip the tour ends it. The first time RazorCAD starts, the start window offers it. If you close the start window on an empty part, it starts by itself, once. Afterwards it is in Help ▸ Getting Started Tour.

sections.title: Search commands
sections.text: Press Ctrl+K (or /), or click the magnifier next to Save, and type part of a command's name: "fil" finds Fillet, "circ pat" Circular Pattern. Pick a result with ↑ / ↓ and Enter, or click it. It searches every command of the menus and the ribbon of the document in front: part, sketch, 3D sketch, assembly or drawing. Each result shows where the command lives (its menu or ribbon tab) and its shortcut. With nothing typed, the commands you used lately come first. Sections of this manual about what you typed are listed after the commands (Manual · and their chapter): pick one to read it in the manual panel.

sections.title: The manual in RazorCAD
sections.text: This manual is built into RazorCAD. Help ▸ User Manual, the ? at the top right of the window or F1 opens it in a panel at the right of the window, beside the model; with a Property panel open, F1 or the panel's ? opens it at that feature. Search: type in the box at its top what you are looking for (a feature, a command, a word): the sections that have all the words are listed, the best first, with the words marked. Click one (or Enter for the first) to read it; the words are marked in it too. The arrows ‹ › go back and forward through what you read; with nothing typed it lists the chapters. Wider or narrower: drag its left edge. RazorCAD keeps the width for next time. A window of its own: ⧉ puts the manual in a window of its own, at the same place. Move it anywhere, onto another monitor too, and size it as you like; help you open while it is open shows there. ⇤ in that window puts it back in the panel; closing that window puts help back in the panel next time. Close: ✕ closes the panel. Your parts, assemblies and drawings stay open as they are; nothing is saved or closed with it.

sections.title: Your own keyboard shortcuts
sections.text: Help ▸ Customize Shortcuts… (or Customize… in Help ▸ Keyboard Shortcuts) gives commands keys of your own. Find a command, click Set and press the keys, for example Ctrl+Shift+F, G or F6. A shortcut works wherever its command is, in the document in front. It takes the place of a key RazorCAD uses itself; the window says when it does (for example F, Zoom to Fit). Giving a key to another command moves it there. Esc, Enter, Tab and Backspace can't be used. ✕ removes a shortcut; Remove All removes them all. Your shortcuts are listed at the top of Help ▸ Keyboard Shortcuts and shown in the command search. They are kept in prefs.json.

sections.title: Using the keyboard
sections.text: The trees: click the feature tree, assembly tree or drawing tree, then ↑ / ↓ move from row to row (selecting as a click does), ← / → close and open folders, Enter opens the item as a double-click does, and Home / End go to the first and last row. While the tree has the keyboard, the arrow keys don't turn the view; click the view to give them back. Property panels: Tab goes through a panel's fields and buttons. The group headings are buttons: Enter or Space opens or closes them. The small ✕ / ▲ buttons in lists can be pressed the same way. Enter on a focused button presses it; elsewhere in the panel it accepts the feature, as before. F6 / Shift+F6 move the keyboard focus round the window: the Property panel (or the tree), the ribbon, the view. Dialogs take the focus when they open (their first field), keep Tab inside, and give the focus back when they close. Screen readers: every panel field is named by its label and unit (for example "Depth (mm)"), fields with an invalid value are marked so, and icon-only buttons are named by their tooltips. The status bar and panel messages are read out as they change, and errors at once.

sections.title: Units
sections.text: Each part, assembly and drawing is in millimetres or inches. Click MMGS / IPS at the right of the status bar, or use Tools ▸ Units: Millimetres / Units: Inches. Changing the units keeps every size exactly as it is; only how sizes are shown and typed changes. In an inch document: Feature fields show and take inches. The arrow keys step 0.1 in (Shift: 1 in). Sketch dimensions, the Modify box and the sizes shown while drawing are in inches. Measure shows in, in² and in³; Mass Properties also gives the mass in pounds. New features start at round sizes, to the nearest 1/8 in. Equation variables used in a length count in inches: with w = 3, a depth of w/2 is 1.5 in. Any value can name its unit: 2in, 30 mm, 1.5cm, 2ft, (w/2)in. Values typed before a document became inch keep their size; an expression typed in millimetres shows as (…)mm. Drawings have units of their own (see the Drawings chapter). A drawing made from an inch part starts in inches.

sections.title: Properties
sections.text: File ▸ Properties… in a part or assembly holds custom properties such as Part Number, Description, Vendor, Finish or Cost. Common names are suggested; any name works. Undo takes a change back. A drawing of the part takes its drawing number from the Part Number, bills of materials can show any property as a column, and the Cost property gives the cost columns (see Bill of Materials).

sections.title: Compare With
sections.text: File ▸ Compare With… compares the part in front with its last saved version, another part file, or another open part. Features and settings: features added or removed, features changed (with which settings: a depth, sketch points, an end condition, a new name), features moved in the tree, and the part's own settings (material, equations, units, configurations, properties). Shapes: both versions' volumes, and the material this version adds (shown yellow on the model) and removes (red), with their volumes.

File ▸ Compare With… compares the part in front with its last saved version, another part file, or another open part.

  • Features and settings: features added or removed, features changed (with which settings: a depth, sketch points, an end condition, a new name), features moved in the tree, and the part's own settings (material, equations, units, configurations, properties).
  • Shapes: both versions' volumes, and the material this version adds (shown yellow on the model) and removes (red), with their volumes.

sections.title: Tabs and closing
sections.text: Several parts and drawings can be open at once, each in its own tab. New, Open and Sample all open a new tab. Closing a tab with unsaved changes asks whether to save it, and closing RazorCAD asks to save every unsaved part.

sections.title: Auto-save and recovery
sections.text: Auto-save starts once a part has been saved for the first time. While the part has unsaved changes it is written next to the part file, at most every 20 seconds, as Name.autosave.rcad. The title bar shows the time of the last auto-save. Saving the part removes the auto-save file. If RazorCAD closes with unsaved changes, opening the part again offers to recover the auto-saved version. It is also marked in the recent list. Warning: A part that was never saved is not auto-saved. RazorCAD warns before closing it. Save new parts early. The recent-files list is kept in %APPDATA%\RazorCAD\recent.json.

sections.title: Opening from Windows and file previews
sections.text: Double-clicking a .rcad, .rasm or .rdrw file opens it in RazorCAD; if RazorCAD is already running, the file opens in a new tab there. RazorCAD sets the file types up itself when it starts. Help ▸ Open Files With RazorCAD… shows whether they are registered and can register them again. Saving keeps a small picture of the view in the file. Windows Explorer, the Open and Save dialogs and the start window show it as the file's thumbnail. A part that takes a while to build is stored, once built, in %LOCALAPPDATA%\RazorCAD\modelcache (kept under 1 GB). With it the kernel keeps the geometry after each feature. Opening the unchanged file again shows the model at once, ready to edit: the first change after opening rebuilds only from the changed feature on, as any later change does. The store is kept for each version of the geometry kernel, so it survives RazorCAD updates that leave the kernel alone. Each open part keeps a geometry kernel of its own, as many as the PC's processor threads and free memory allow (see Speed on your PC in the Troubleshooting chapter). Switching back to a part is then immediate, and a part still building goes on while you work in another tab.

sections.title: Point clouds
sections.text: File ▸ Import Point Cloud (PLY, XYZ)… brings a scan into the part as a Point Cloud feature, shown as dots: a PLY file (ASCII or binary; its faces are not read) or a text file of x y z lines (XYZ, TXT, CSV, PTS). Up to 200 000 points are kept (every so many of a bigger scan). Surfaces ▸ Fit Surface to Points makes a surface body fitted to it by least squares: a Plane, a Cylinder, a Sphere, or a Freeform surface through a grid of heights over the cloud's best plane (more grid points follow it more closely). The message gives how far the points are from the surface (RMS and the largest). Build the part on the fitted surfaces with the usual tools (Thicken, Knit, Replace Face…).

sections.title: Importing STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ and 3MF
sections.text: There are two ways to bring in a STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ or 3MF file: File ▸ Open… opens it as a part of its own in a new tab, named after the file, without asking. A STEP file that holds an assembly asks first: Open as an Assembly makes a new assembly with the file's structure: a sub-assembly for each of its sub-assemblies, a part for each part, and a component, fixed, where the file places each one. Each part keeps its own piece of the STEP file and is built on its own, and a part used several times is built once. The first build of each part is kept on disk (in %LOCALAPPDATA%\RazorCAD\modelcache, up to 1 GB, shared with parts). The next time the assembly opens, unchanged parts are shown straight from there instead of being rebuilt, so a big assembly reopens in seconds. Open as One Part brings every solid into one part, as before. File ▸ Import STEP / STL… (Ctrl+I, also on the Features tab, and Import STEP / STL / OBJ / 3MF on the Evaluate tab) offers three choices: a new part, insert in place into the current part, or insert and locate with mates. Locating with mates adds a separate "Locate …" Move Body feature under the import. How imports behave: The file's contents are stored inside the part file, so the part does not depend on the original file. A STEP file's appearances come with it: the colour of each solid and of single faces, and transparency. Your own Appearance and Make Transparent / Make Opaque settings on a body win over them. STEP imports as an exact solid. Every solid becomes its own body; a solid made of several separate shells is split into one body per shell; loose surfaces become surface bodies. The bodies of a multi-body STEP file are grouped in their own folder under Solid Bodies. Tick Merge touching bodies into one body in the import feature to fuse them instead. STL, OBJ and 3MF meshes are converted to a solid made of their triangles, with coplanar triangles merged. A 3MF file's units and build placement are read. A mesh that is not closed comes in as a surface body, with a note saying how many open edges it has; Repair Mesh or Convert to Solid (Surfaces chapter) can close it. Big meshes are simplified on import, by default to 80,000 triangles, keeping their edges and outlines. Set the limit in the import's properties (Simplify meshes above … triangles; 0 never simplifies). The import's note says how far a mesh was simplified. Imported bodies can be cut, extended, patterned and (for STEP) filleted like any other body. A cut or fillet on a body of more than 20,000 mesh faces warns that it can take several minutes. IGES files (.igs, .iges) open and import like STEP files. Trimmed and bounded surfaces, B-rep solids, B-spline, plane, revolved, extruded, cylinder, cone, sphere and torus surfaces, lines, arcs, B-spline and composite curves and polylines are read, with the file's units and transformations. Faces that close up are sewn into a solid; the rest come in as surface bodies. RazorCAD translates IGES into STEP for the geometry kernel, which has no IGES reader of its own. Volumes of bodies with B-spline faces (imported NURBS, IGES) are measured exactly.

sections.title: Export Face as DXF
sections.text: Click a flat face, then right-click ▸ Export Face as DXF… (or File ▸ Export ▸ Face as DXF…). The face's outline (layer OUTLINE) and holes (layer HOLES) are written as a 2D drawing in millimetres, seen from outside the part. Use it for laser or waterjet cutting, or to take a profile into a 2D CAD program. Lines, arcs and circles are exact; other curves become fine polylines. The file is DXF R12, which practically every program can read.

sections.title: Up axis: Y or Z
sections.text: A part can be shown Y up (the default) or Z up: View ▸ Up Axis, right-click Origin in the feature tree, or click Y up / Z up at the right of the status bar. With Z up the Top plane is XY, the Front plane XZ and the Right plane YZ, and Z points up; the tree shows each standard plane's axes beside its name. The choice is kept with the part and used for new parts too. Only the names of the axes change: the model stays where it is and no feature moves. The triad, X / Y / Z directions, Move / Copy Bodies, reference point coordinates, Measure, Mass Properties and 3D sketch coordinates all use the part's axes, and so do exported STEP, STL, OBJ and 3MF files: a part shown Z up is written Z up, and a file imported into it is read Z up. The origin and corner triad always show X in red, Y in green and Z in blue: the vertical axis is green with Y up and blue with Z up. An assembly keeps its own up axis in the same way (View ▸ Up Axis, the status bar, or right-click its Origin in the tree; Undo takes it back). Its tree shows the standard planes' axes, and a STEP file exported from an assembly shown Z up is written Z up. A new assembly starts with the up axis used for new parts.

sections.title: Visibility
sections.text: View ▸ Show / Hide Planes toggles the standard planes. The eye column at the right of the Feature tree shows or hides each sketch, plane, axis, point, curve, body and body-making feature on its own. Hiding a feature hides the bodies it built. Planes, axes, points and curves can also be hidden one at a time with right-click ▸ Hide. The eye button on the heads-up toolbar (or View ▸ Visibility…) filters what is shown: sketches, axes, planes, points and surfaces, with select-all and deselect-all. Right-click a body (tree or view) ▸ Hide. Tab hides the body under the cursor; Shift+Tab shows the hidden body under the cursor. View ▸ Show Hidden Bodies shows hidden bodies so you can click them to show them again. Choose Done Showing Hidden Bodies to finish. Right-click a body ▸ Isolate hides everything else. The isolated body can still be edited. View ▸ Exit Isolate returns. Right-click a body, or any feature that made or changed it, ▸ Make Transparent / Make Opaque. Transparency is saved with the part and can be undone.

sections.title: Section view
sections.text: Tools ▸ Section View… (or the Evaluate tab) cuts the model open on a plane so you can see inside. Choose the plane, an offset (equations are allowed) and flip the side kept. With a flat face, a plane or a sketch selected when you start, the cut starts on it; while the panel is open, click a flat face or a plane to cut from it instead. Drag the blue arrow on the cut to move it along its normal (the offset follows, in round steps; looking straight along it, drag up to bring it toward you). Tick Section 2 (and Section 3) to cut with two or three planes at once: only what all of them cut away is removed, e.g. a quarter cut. The arrow and a click in the view move the section you changed last. It works the same in assemblies (Evaluate ▸ Section View): every component is cut and capped, and a click on a component's flat face cuts from it. ✓ keeps the cut on while you work; the Section View button then opens the panel again, and ✗ removes the cut. Saved with a cut on, a part or assembly opens with it again, and each tab keeps its own cut. Each cut body or component gets its own cap in its colour, outlined and hatched with section lines; the hatch angle and spacing change from body to body so touching parts read apart. Section View can't be used inside a sketch.

sections.title: Quick readout of sizes
sections.text: Clicking an edge shows a small tag in the view: its length, R and length for an arc, or Ø and circumference for a circle. Ctrl+click more edges for their total length (the perimeter when they go all the way round). Sketch entities shown in the view can be clicked the same way. One face shows its area (and Ø when round). Ctrl+click a second face for how they lie: "Parallel · 12 mm apart", "Perpendicular · 90°" or the angle; two round faces give their centre distance; three or more faces their total area.
sections.html:

One face shows its area (and Ø when round). Ctrl+click a second face for how they lie: "Parallel · 12 mm apart", "Perpendicular · 90°" or the angle; two round faces give their centre distance; three or more faces their total area.

sections.title: Highlighting from the tree
sections.text: Hovering a feature in the Feature tree highlights what it made in orange: the faces of a boss, cut, fillet, chamfer, shell, pattern or moved body; a sketch's curves; a plane, axis or point; a surface feature's surfaces. Clicking it keeps the highlight in blue while it is selected.

sections.title: Selecting hidden bodies
sections.text: Hold Shift and right-click to step through the bodies and surfaces under the cursor, front to back; Shift + left-click steps back. The current one is shown in orange, through whatever is in front of it. Release Shift and left-click on the same spot to select it. Esc or a click elsewhere cancels. With only the face filter on, or while a Property panel asks for faces (Shell, Offset Surface), it steps through faces instead. While a Property panel asks for bodies (Combine, Split, Move/Copy, Knit, Thicken), the click adds the body.

sections.title: Starting and ending a sketch
sections.text: Click a plane or a flat face, then click Sketch (Sketch tab), or right-click a face ▸ Sketch. Clicking a sketch tool such as Circle with no sketch open also starts a 2D sketch: pick a plane or flat face and the tool is ready. (For sketches in space, see the 3D Sketches chapter.) You can also start a feature such as Extrude without a sketch: RazorCAD asks you to pick a plane or face, you sketch, and when you exit the sketch the feature continues. If the profile is open you can keep editing or abort and keep the sketch. Esc ends the active sketch tool first; pressing it again closes the sketch and keeps it. Enter does not leave the sketch. The ✔ in the confirm corner, or Exit Sketch, closes the sketch. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo inside the sketch.

sections.title: The sketch tool wheel
sections.text: While sketching, press and hold the right mouse button. After a moment, or as soon as you start to drag, a wheel of sketch tools appears around the pointer. Keep the button held, move toward a tool (it highlights) and release to activate it. Releasing in the centre or pressing Esc cancels. A quick right click (press and release without moving) still opens the right-click menu.

sections.title: Defined and under-defined sketches
sections.text: Sketches are made of points, lines, arcs and circles held in place by relations and dimensions. A numerical constraint solver keeps them satisfied. Geometry is blue when under-defined and black when fully defined. The Property panel shows the remaining degrees of freedom. An under-defined sketch shows (-) in the tree. Construction lines only need to be positioned. To rename a sketch, right-click its tree item and choose Rename, including when it has the (-) marker.

sections.title: Automatic relations
sections.text: With Automatic relations while sketching enabled, Line and Centerline infer parallel or collinear directions from other lines in the active sketch, including construction and projected lines. The reference highlights orange and the cursor identifies the proposed relation. Click to create a persistent relation. Starting near a line's extension snaps onto its supporting line; continuing along it creates Collinear. Endpoint, midpoint and on-curve snaps retain priority. Direction inference uses a 4° angular tolerance and a 9-pixel proximity limit; spline control-polygon helpers are excluded. Turning automatic relations off disables these inferences.

sections.title: Sketch orientation
sections.text: In the sketch Property panel, Rotate 90° turns the sketch axes about the sketch normal, and Flip Side looks at the sketch from the other side of the plane. Both are saved with the sketch.

sections.title: Sketch tools
sections.text: Tool Key How it works --- --- --- Select S Select entities, drag geometry Line L Click a chain of points. Coincident, horizontal, vertical, parallel and collinear relations are inferred automatically; snapping to a midpoint or onto a curve adds those relations too. Double-click, Enter or Esc ends the chain. Centerline Construction line for symmetry, mirroring, gears or as a revolve axis Midpoint Line Midpoint, then one endpoint; the opposite endpoint is mirrored and a Midpoint relation preserves the centre Corner Rectangle R Built with horizontal and vertical relations Center Rectangle Also adds construction diagonals with a midpoint relation Circle C Centre, then radius Centerpoint Arc A Centre, start, end; the direction follows the mouse 3 Point Arc Start, end, then a point it runs through Tangent Arc From the end of a line or arc, kept tangent by a Tangent relation Ellipse Centre, end of the major axis, then the minor radius. Trim it for an elliptical arc. Fit Point Spline N Through fit points, with editable tangent direction and strength handles; see below Point Lone sketch points that stay, for example to place holes Straight Slot Built with tangent and equal relations Center Point Slot Slot midpoint, one end-arc centre, then width Overall Slot Two outermost points along the axis define total length; the third click defines width Center Point Arc Slot Centre of the path arc, start centre, end direction, then width 3 Point Arc Slot Start centre, end centre, third point on the centre arc, then width Polygon P Set the number of sides in the Property panel Dimension D See below Trim T See below Extend A line or arc end runs on to the first entity in its way and stays on it Split Splits a line or arc in two at the click; the halves stay collinear or equal Project Edges E See below Offset O See below Mirror Select the entities plus a centerline, then click Mirror Import DXF See below Sketch Picture A picture (PNG, JPEG, BMP, GIF or WebP) on the sketch plane, to trace over. See below Equation Curve A spline through the points of y = f(x) (x from / to) or of x = f(t), y = g(t) (t from / to), in a number of Pieces. Part variables can be used and the curve follows them; sin, cos and tan take degrees. A parametric curve that ends where it starts is closed. An Equation relation holds it (it is fully defined); select it and use Equation Curve again to change it. Linear Sketch Pattern Opens a side panel with an orange preview. Select source entities before or after opening it, then choose an angle, line or curve as direction/path. Copies stay linked to their sources, path, quantity and spacing. Along a curve, spacing is measured along it and copies can rotate with it; open paths stop at their end. A straight direction also supports a second direction. Circular Sketch Pattern Copies the selected entities with the relations and dimensions among them. A selected point is the pattern's centre. Make Block / Insert Block / Explode Block Make Block saves the selection (with its relations) under a name in your settings. Insert Block places copies with a click, in any sketch, turned by an angle, and can delete blocks from the library. A linked copy (the default) moves and turns as one (a rigid Block relation holds it) and follows the block: Make Block again under the same name updates every copy in the sketch where it is, keeping relations from other geometry to it. Explode Block makes the selected copies plain geometry with the block's own relations and dimensions. Untick Linked for plain copies. Text See below Gears See the Gears chapter Airfoil See the Airfoils chapter Sketch Fillet / Sketch Chamfer Set the radius or distance, then click corners (a fillet: where two lines, a line and an arc, two arcs, or a fit-point spline and a line or an arc meet: the spline is cut back to the fillet, which stays tangent to it; a chamfer: two lines). The first one made gets the dimension; the others made before you leave the tool are made Equal to it, so one value changes them all. Intersection Curve Click earlier sketch curves to create linked intersections with the active sketch plane, or select a model section Construction Geometry Q Toggles selected curves to/from construction; with no curves selected, toggles construction mode for newly drawn geometry. The drawing panel also has For construction. Preview and resulting geometry are dashed and ignored by features. Display Relations Shows or hides the relation glyphs Delete Del Deletes the selected entities or relations Linear patterns and patterns along a path: confirm with the checkmark, or cancel with the cross (Enter / Esc also work outside input fields). The preview does not change the sketch until confirmed. Use Sketch Patterns ▸ Edit Pattern in the sketch Property panel to change sources, path, count, spacing or rotation later; count and spacing accept expressions. Edit original geometry to change the copies' shapes. Copies are linked and cannot be independently dragged; deleting a source, path or generated entity removes that pattern's copies. Parameters and links are kept with the part and follow undo/redo and rebuilds. Patterns made by earlier versions were independent copies and contain no stored pattern definition. Recreate them with the updated command to obtain a parametric pattern. Pattern copies use the defined-geometry colour: black in the light theme and light in the dark theme. Purple identifies projected geometry; the pattern preview is orange. Fillet corners can share one endpoint or have endpoints joined by Coincident relations. If exactly two regular lines/arcs meet at a corner, construction geometry there is ignored when choosing the curves to fillet. An invalid radius leaves the sketch unchanged.

Linear patterns and patterns along a path: confirm with the checkmark, or cancel with the cross (Enter / Esc also work outside input fields). The preview does not change the sketch until confirmed. sections.title: Dimension
sections.text: Click a line, circle or arc (or two entities), then click to place the dimension. You can also select a curve or two entities before starting Dimension. Move the pointer to position the orange preview, then click to confirm; the dimension is not created until that click. Press Esc to cancel the pending dimension. The text is placed at the point you choose. With Select or Dimension active, drag a dimension's number to reposition its annotation without changing the measured geometry or value. A plain click still opens the value editor. This also works for driven/reference dimensions; placement is saved with the sketch and follows undo/redo. Press Esc during a drag to cancel the move. Linear dimension text follows the dimension line and stays upright. Extension lines leave a small gap at the geometry and run slightly beyond the dimension line; short dimensions use outside arrows. For a point-to-line distance, dragging the text also moves the perpendicular dimension line along the reference edge. This lets a short horizontal offset such as 4 mm and an inclined perpendicular offset such as 13 mm use conventional drafting layouts without changing what they measure. Moving the mouse switches between horizontal, vertical and aligned. Two lines give an angle; a point and a line give a perpendicular distance. Values accept equations, such as width/2. A dimension that would over-define the sketch is added as a driven (reference) dimension. Circles and arcs: dimension from a circle or arc to another circle, arc, point or line by clicking both. The Modify box offers Center (centre to centre), Min (nearest) and Max (farthest). Min also measures the gap between concentric circles. Switching keeps the geometry in place and shows the new value. Outside references: you can also click model edges, model vertices or entities of earlier sketches. RazorCAD creates linked construction geometry and dimensions to it, so the dimension follows the model. Example: "keep this hole 25 mm from the right edge" still holds after the width changes.

You can also select a curve or two entities before starting Dimension. Move the pointer to position the orange preview, then click to confirm; the dimension is not created until that click. Press Esc to cancel the pending dimension. The text is placed at the point you choose.

With Select or Dimension active, drag a dimension's number to reposition its annotation without changing the measured geometry or value. A plain click still opens the value editor. This also works for driven/reference dimensions; placement is saved with the sketch and follows undo/redo. Press Esc during a drag to cancel the move.

For a point-to-line distance, dragging the text also moves the perpendicular dimension line along the reference edge. This lets a short horizontal offset such as 4 mm and an inclined perpendicular offset such as 13 mm use conventional drafting layouts without changing what they measure.

  • Moving the mouse switches between horizontal, vertical and aligned.
  • Two lines give an angle; a point and a line give a perpendicular distance.
  • Values accept equations, such as width/2.
  • A dimension that would over-define the sketch is added as a driven (reference) dimension.
  • Circles and arcs: dimension from a circle or arc to another circle, arc, point or line by clicking both. The Modify box offers Center (centre to centre), Min (nearest) and Max (farthest). Min also measures the gap between concentric circles. Switching keeps the geometry in place and shows the new value.
  • Outside references: you can also click model edges, model vertices or entities of earlier sketches. RazorCAD creates linked construction geometry and dimensions to it, so the dimension follows the model. Example: "keep this hole 25 mm from the right edge" still holds after the width changes.

sections.title: Trim
sections.text: Power trim: hover over a segment and it turns red; click to remove it up to the nearest intersections. Lines are shortened or split, circles become arcs, and new end points get on-curve relations.
sections.html: Power trim: hover over a segment and it turns red; click to remove it up to the nearest intersections. Lines are shortened or split, circles become arcs, and new end points get on-curve relations.

sections.title: Offset
sections.text: Click a line, arc, circle or spline, choose the options in the Property panel, then click to create its offset. Select chain switches between the clicked entity and its connected contour, including mixed line/arc/spline chains. Corners are re-trimmed or extended; an unjoinable or collapsed offset reports an error. Direction offers Pick side, Inside / left, Outside / right and Both sides. Inside and outside follow the winding of a closed contour, including reversed contours. For an open chain they mean left and right along its traversal. Both sides places a copy at the specified distance on each side: one dimension drives both copies, so the total separation is twice the distance. Enter Distance before creating the offset; expressions and parameters are supported. Use mouse distance lets the pointer set the initial distance instead. The resulting offset dimension can be edited later. Linked offsets retain their source references through save/reopen and follow source edits. Constrain the source geometry to hold it in place while changing dimensions. Line and arc offsets remain analytic. Spline parallels are represented by cubic spline pieces, checked against source-curve normals at sampled parameters within 0.001 mm; this is a sampled numerical check, not a certified global bound. Cusps, detected crossings and folds are rejected. A large source edit that exceeds the stored fit tolerance asks you to recreate that offset. Ellipses are not supported. Copies and blocks retain plain geometry rather than the offset link. You can also click a model edge (with Select chain, the connected edges lying in a plane parallel to the sketch, such as a face outline) or a curve of another sketch. Linked offset (default): the offset follows its source, including model edges when the model changes, and one dimension drives the chain (relation "Offset ⇉"). Untick it for a single offset: plain geometry with no link. While the tool is active, the faces the sketch plane cuts are highlighted and the cut outline is drawn in teal. Clicking it offsets the whole outline.

sections.title: Project Edges
sections.text: While editing a source sketch, sketches that depend on it are temporarily hidden to avoid displaying outdated projections over the current geometry. They return after leaving the sketch and rebuilding; independent reference sketches remain visible and the saved visibility settings are unchanged. If a source edit such as a fillet separates formerly joined endpoints, their projected endpoints separate on rebuild while retaining their source links. Splines projected from another sketch remain linked splines, preserving their control points, degree and weights. Earlier projections saved as line segments retain that representation. Click a model edge, or an entity of an earlier sketch, to project it into this sketch. Or select edges first and then click Project Edges (or press E): they are projected at once. Projected geometry is drawn in purple, is linked and updates when the source changes (relation "On Edge ⇲"). The ends of projected lines are joined to each other and to sketch geometry already there, so the edges of a face give a closed outline ready to extrude. While the tool is active, the outline where the sketch plane cuts the bodies is drawn in teal; clicking it converts the whole outline. This works for solids and surfaces.

Click a model edge, or an entity of an earlier sketch, to project it into this sketch. Or select edges first and then click Project Edges (or press E): they are projected at once. sections.title: Selecting source sketches for Project and Intersection
sections.text: While editing a sketch, activate Project Edges or Intersection Curve. Earlier independent sketches are temporarily shown, including hidden and absorbed sketches; their saved visibility does not change. Click the source curves in the canvas (orbit the view if they overlap). Project creates linked projected geometry. Intersection creates linked points where source lines, arcs, circles or splines cross the active plane (a spline's crossings are solved on its exact curve, every one it makes); coplanar curves retain their geometry. Use the points as guide endpoints. For solid/surface sections, click the displayed section outline. Escape returns to Select. Projection Source → Source can restrict picking to one earlier sketch or to model edges/sections. Choose the intended sketch when several sources overlap in the view. Other source sketches are temporarily hidden; leaving the tool restores their saved visibility. Source geometry is gray, while projected entities are purple. A visible source edge joining two projected sides is not automatically added to the active sketch.

sections.title: Spline
sections.text: New Fit Point Splines include a tangent handle at each fit point. Drag a handle to change tangent direction and strength; adjacent pieces keep the same tangent through their shared fit point. Dragging a fit point carries its handle with it. Handle lines are construction geometry and accept ordinary line constraints and dimensions (for example horizontal, parallel, length or angle). Their remaining freedoms count towards sketch definition. Copies, mirrors, blocks, patterns and linked projections preserve the handles. Existing saved splines retain their previous representation. Tangent handles are shown with solid teal stems, small direction arrows and round grips. Fit points use square markers. Selection names identify Tangent Handle and Tangent Handle Line, so these controls can be distinguished from ordinary construction centre lines. Click the points the curve runs through (they snap like line points), then double-click, Enter or Esc to finish, or click the first point again to close it. Drag a point to reshape the curve, or drag the curve to move it; deleting a point takes it out of the spline. Convert to Control-Point Spline (in its panel) makes it a control-point spline that runs through the same points. Splines make profiles on their own or with lines and arcs and are exact curves for extrudes, revolves, cuts, lofts and sweep paths. Lines can be trimmed where they cross a spline.
sections.html:
New Fit Point Splines include a tangent handle at each fit point. Drag a handle to change tangent direction and strength; adjacent pieces keep the same tangent through their shared fit point. Dragging a fit point carries its handle with it. Handle lines are construction geometry and accept ordinary line constraints and dimensions (for example horizontal, parallel, length or angle). Their remaining freedoms count towards sketch definition. Copies, mirrors, blocks, patterns and linked projections preserve the handles. Existing saved splines retain their previous representation.

Tangent handles are shown with solid teal stems, small direction arrows and round grips. Fit points use square markers. Selection names identify Tangent Handle and Tangent Handle Line, so these controls can be distinguished from ordinary construction centre lines.

Click the points the curve runs through (they snap like line points), then double-click, Enter or Esc to finish, or click the first point again to close it. Drag a point to reshape the curve, or drag the curve to move it; deleting a point takes it out of the spline. Convert to Control-Point Spline (in its panel) makes it a control-point spline that runs through the same points. Splines make profiles on their own or with lines and arcs and are exact curves for extrudes, revolves, cuts, lofts and sweep paths. Lines can be trimmed where they cross a spline.

sections.title: Control-Point Spline
sections.text: Control-Point Spline (beside Spline) draws a spline from control points: click them, then double-click, Enter or Esc to finish (click the first point again to close it: it then runs round smoothly, with no join). An open one starts and ends on the first and last control points and passes near the others; a closed one passes near them all. The Closed box in its panel opens or closes it. Choose the degree (1 to 7) in the panel before drawing, or select the spline afterwards to change it (at most one less than the control points): a higher degree is smoother and keeps farther from the polygon. The control polygon is drawn dashed and is made of construction lines, so you can dimension it and give it relations like any lines: horizontal, parallel, equal, an angle. The curve leaves each end along the polygon's end leg, so a relation on that leg (tangent to an arc, collinear with a line) sets its direction there. Drag the control points to reshape it. Deleting the spline deletes its polygon. Select a control point for its own settings. Weight (1 is plain) pulls the curve toward that point when larger and lets it go farther when smaller: with three control points at the corners of a square, degree 2 and a weight of 0.7071 on the middle one, the curve is a quarter circle (to within 0.00001 mm). Insert After adds a control point half way along the next leg (the curve changes shape a little); Remove, or deleting the point, takes it out and joins its two legs.

sections.title: Import DXF
sections.text: Import DXF brings a DXF file into the open sketch: lines, arcs, circles, polylines with arcs, ellipses and elliptical arcs, splines, points and blocks. The file's units are converted to millimetres. You can scale it and place it as in the file, centred, or by its corner. Sketch Picture puts a picture on the sketch plane behind the sketch, to trace over (a photo, a scan of a drawing). Set its width (the height follows), centre, angle, opacity, or hide it. To scale it by something of known size in it, draw a line along that, select the line, open Sketch Picture again, pick the picture and give the line's true length: the picture is scaled about the line's start. Pictures are shown while you edit the sketch, are saved in the part (shrunk to 2000 pixels across at most) and are not geometry: they make no faces and are not exported.

sections.title: Text
sections.text: Click Text on the Sketch tab, then click to place. The panel sets the text, font (the PC's installed fonts, and the DejaVu Sans, Sans Mono and Serif fonts that come with RazorCAD), height (capital-letter height), angle, bold and italic. A font a PC doesn't have is drawn in the DejaVu font most like it. Drag the text to move it. Text extrudes as a boss or cut; text inside an outline is cut out of it. To put text on a curved face, use Wrap (Features chapter).

sections.title: Relations
sections.text: Select entities (Ctrl+click for several, or drag a box from empty space: left to right selects what lies wholly inside it, right to left whatever it touches; Ctrl or Shift adds). The Property panel lists the relations that apply: Selection Relations offered --- --- 1 line Horizontal, Vertical, Fixed 2 or more points Coincident, Horizontal, Vertical 2 or more lines Parallel, Perpendicular, Collinear, Equal, Horizontal, Vertical Point + line Coincident (on line), Midpoint Point + arc Coincident (on curve), Midpoint (half way round the arc) Point + circle Coincident (on curve) Line + circle/arc Tangent Line + open spline Tangent at a spline endpoint (control-point or fit-point spline) Circles/arcs Equal Radius, Equal Curve Length, Concentric, Tangent 2 or more curves (including splines, ellipses or mixed line/curve selections) Equal Curve Length; for lines only, use Equal 2 points + line Symmetric (about the line) 3 lines Symmetric (two lines about a centerline) Relations are shown as small green glyphs next to the geometry. Click a glyph to select it, then press Del to remove it. Hovering a glyph highlights the entities it ties together. For several selected entities, relations already implied by existing constraints are skipped while useful relations are added. A relation refused says why: one that is already satisfied names the relations that already define the geometry that way (an information message); one that would over-define the sketch names the relations or dimensions in its way. Either way those relations are selected, so you can delete one and add the new relation instead. A true conflict rejects the entire request without changing the sketch. Tangent with a spline: Ctrl-select a line and an open spline, then choose Tangent. The shared endpoint, or otherwise the spline endpoint closest to the infinite line, is used. To choose explicitly (required if both ends are equally close), also select the desired spline endpoint. The selected endpoint is stored and does not switch after edits. For control-point splines the first or last control-polygon leg is aligned with the line; fit-point splines use their endpoint tangent. Coincidence is separate: add Coincident between endpoints or Coincident (on line) to make the curves meet. Closed splines and zero-length endpoint directions are unsupported. Equal Curve Length (≋) constrains the length measured along each selected curve, not its chord or control polygon. Two arcs may have different radii and sweeps while keeping equal lengths; a spline can also match a line or another curve. Select the curves with Ctrl and choose Equal Curve Length in Add Relations. With more than two curves, each is matched to the first. Circular curves' Equal Radius (=) keeps their radii equal and remains a separate relation. Length links survive source edits, undo/redo, save/reopen and rebuild. Ellipse and spline lengths are integrated numerically from their definitions.

sections.title: How profiles are found
sections.text: Profiles are found automatically from all non-construction geometry and sent to the kernel as exact lines, arcs and circles. Intersections are split, dangling lines are ignored and nested loops become holes. A full circle (or arcs that make one) becomes a single closed curve, so an extruded circle has one continuous cylindrical face. For canvas region selection, connected lines, arcs and splines can divide a closed outline into separate selectable cells within the same sketch. Click inside the desired cell; shared boundary edges may belong to several cells. Holes remain attached to their enclosing cell and can also be selected as disks. New cell references preserve boundary direction so regions sharing the same source curve IDs remain distinct. Existing whole-sketch and saved outline selections retain their previous extent. Construction geometry does not subdivide regions.

sections.title: Showing and hiding sketches
sections.text: Sketches absorbed by a feature are hidden by default. Right-click a sketch in the tree ▸ Show / Hide, or use its eye in the tree.

sections.title: Change Sketch Plane
sections.text: Right-click a sketch ▸ Change Sketch Plane… and pick another plane or flat face for it, for example to repair a sketch whose plane was deleted ("The reference plane is missing"). Its curves keep their sketch coordinates. Only planes above the sketch in the tree are offered.

sections.title: 3D Sketches
sections.text: A 3D sketch holds lines, arcs, circles and splines in space rather than on one plane. Use it for frames (see the Fast Structure chapter), pipe, duct and wiring routes, and sweep paths.
sections.html: A 3D sketch holds lines, arcs, circles and splines in space rather than on one plane. Use it for frames (see the Fast Structure chapter), pipe, duct and wiring routes, and sweep paths.

sections.title: Starting and ending a 3D sketch
sections.text: Click 3D Sketch on the Sketch tab or the Fast Structure tab (or Insert ▸ 3D Sketch). The sketch opens empty with the Line tool ready; there is no plane to pick. While it is open the 3D Sketch button stays highlighted and the first button becomes Exit 3D Sketch. Tools that only work in 2D sketches are greyed out. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo inside the sketch.

sections.title: Drawing in space
sections.text: Click points to draw lines. A line snaps along X, Y or Z from the last point whenever the mouse moves along that direction on screen, in any view. A dashed line shows it and an Along X/Y/Z relation is added. Hold Ctrl or Shift to draw freely. Away from the axes, lines follow the drawing plane through the last point. Tab cycles XY → YZ → ZX; the plane's name shows at the cursor. Ctrl+click a plane or flat face, or click a plane in the tree, to draw on it. Points placed there get an On Plane relation. Tab or Esc goes back to XY / YZ / ZX. Points snap, in this order, to the sketch's own points, to line and arc midpoints (Midpoint relation), to a point along a line (On Line relation), to the origin and model vertices, along X/Y/Z, then to the drawing plane. The Next Point box in the Property panel takes exact offsets, for example 0, 0, 250. A selected point shows its X, Y and Z; type new values to move it. A selected line shows its length, ΔX/ΔY/ΔZ and end points; an arc its radius, angle and length.

sections.title: Projected edges in 3D
sections.text: Project Edges brings model edges into the 3D sketch: lines stay lines, circular edges become arcs or circles and other curves become splines, with shared corner points. The geometry (purple) stays linked to the model: when the part changes, it follows the edges, and lines and dimensions attached to it follow too. Unlink from the Model in the Property panel makes it ordinary geometry.

sections.title: Curves from a 3D sketch
sections.text: Each connected run of lines, arcs and splines is one curve; a T-junction splits it into separate runs. A run can be used as straight segments with an optional bend radius at the corners (pipe and duct routes) or as a smooth spline, and can be closed into a loop. Sweep, Swept Surface, Lofted Surface, Curve Driven Pattern and Structural Member use 3D sketches.

sections.title: Gears
sections.text: RazorCAD's Gears tool on the Sketch tab draws involute gear trains as closed profiles, ready to extrude.
sections.html: RazorCAD's Gears tool on the Sketch tab draws involute gear trains as closed profiles, ready to extrude.

sections.title: Creating a gear train
sections.text: Draw lines between the gear centres (centerlines work well). Select the lines (or a single point for one gear) and click Gears. If you are not in a sketch, RazorCAD opens the selected sketch (or starts one) and asks you to click the centre lines, then press Enter or Make Gears. Each line end point becomes a gear. Neighbouring gears mesh along the line, and teeth are turned automatically so they mesh. Extrude the sketch: each gear becomes its own body. Gear numbers are shown on the gears in the sketch (view labels only, not geometry).

  4. Extrude the sketch: each gear becomes its own body.

sections.title: Rules for a valid train
sections.text: Centres must be exactly at the mesh distance, gears must not overlap and each gear needs at least 6 teeth. Fixed line lengths get a module and teeth that fit. Edits that would break a train are refused. A broken train is drawn red with a Fit gears to the lines button and can't be extruded.

sections.title: Drawing an airfoil
sections.text: Select a line in a sketch and click Airfoil (or click Airfoil, then the line). The line becomes the chord: a construction line with the leading edge at its start. The airfoil is drawn on it. The airfoil follows the line. Drag its ends or dimension it (or set Chord length in the panel) and the airfoil scales and turns with it. Extrude the sketch. The profile is one smooth closed curve that follows the exact section to within 0.002 % of the chord.

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.text: This tutorial builds a small duct and a tray with tools added in the 0.17 versions: the closed control-point spline, a plane placed with Placement, a loft that follows a guide curve, a variable fillet with a point along its edge, and edge flanges that meet corner to corner. The finished part is in File ▸ Open Example Part (Tutorial) (also on the start window): open it to look round, or follow the steps in a new part.

The finished part is in File ▸ Open Example Part (Tutorial) (also on the start window): open it to look round, or follow the steps in a new part.

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: The bottom profile
sections.text: Select the Top Plane and click Sketch. Click Control-Point Spline on the Sketch tab and click eight control points round the origin, roughly at (50, 0), (40, 25), (0, 30), (−40, 25), (−50, 0), (−40, −25), (0, −30) and (40, −25). Click the first point again to close it: the curve runs round smoothly, near the points rather than through them. Select the spline: its panel shows the Degree (3) and the Closed box. Select a control point to see its Weight; leave it at 1 for now. Drag a control point and the curve follows. Exit the sketch.
sections.html:
1. Select the Top Plane and click Sketch.
  2. Click Control-Point Spline on the Sketch tab and click eight control points round the origin, roughly at (50, 0), (40, 25), (0, 30), (−40, 25), (−50, 0), (−40, −25), (0, −30) and (40, −25). Click the first point again to close it: the curve runs round smoothly, near the points rather than through them.
  3. Select the spline: its panel shows the Degree (3) and the Closed box. Select a control point to see its Weight; leave it at 1 for now. Drag a control point and the curve follows.
  4. Exit the sketch.

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: A plane, moved and turned
sections.text: Click Reference Plane, pick the Top Plane and set the offset to 100. Under Placement, set Turn its axes in the plane to 30°: the plane's axes turn in the plane, so whatever is sketched on it turns with them. Sketch a circle of radius 20 at the origin on this plane and exit the sketch.

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: The guide curve
sections.text: Sketch on the Front Plane. With Control-Point Spline, click three points: the first where the bottom profile crosses the X axis (about 46.67, 0), one out to the side (about 62, 45) and the last on the circle (20, 100). Finish with a double-click or Enter. A guide curve has to touch every profile. The first point lies on the bottom profile's curve, not on a control point: with these control points the curve crosses the axis at 140/3 = 46.6667 mm (select the point and type 46.6667 for its X in the panel).

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: The guided loft
sections.text: Click Loft, pick the bottom sketch and then the circle's sketch as the profiles. Under Guide Curves, pick the guide sketch. The loft's side follows the guide between the two profiles, and the profiles stay exactly as drawn. The note reads "2 profiles, 1 guide curve".

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: A fillet with a point along its edge
sections.text: Click Fillet, set the type to Variable size and Radius to At vertices and points along edges, and click the loft's bottom edge where the guide starts. Set the radius to 3: that is the radius at the edge's vertices. Under Points along the edges, click Add Point: half way along the edge (50 %) with a radius of 8. The point is marked on the edge; the fillet swells smoothly from 3 at the vertices to 8 there.
sections.html:
1. Click Fillet, set the type to Variable size and Radius to At vertices and points along edges, and click the loft's bottom edge where the guide starts.
  2. Set the radius to 3: that is the radius at the edge's vertices.
  3. Under Points along the edges, click Add Point: half way along the edge (50 %) with a radius of 8. The point is marked on the edge; the fillet swells smoothly from 3 at the vertices to 8 there.

sections.chapter: Tutorial: a Guided Loft and a Sheet Metal Tray
sections.title: The tray
sections.text: Sketch an 80 × 60 rectangle on the Top Plane, beside the duct, and click Base Flange on the Sheet Metal tab with a thickness of 1.5 mm. Click Edge Flange and pick the four top edges, with a length of 20. Under Corners, Corner to corner is the default: where two flanges meet, each runs on up to the other's inside face and ends square, the gap apart, and the bends end in a small V cutout. Mitred would close them on the diagonal, and Overlap would run one flange past the other's end. Click Flatten to see the tray laid out, with its bend lines. Tip: change any value in the tree (the spline's degree, a weight, the plane's turn, the fillet's point) and the part rebuilds from there.

sections.title: Live previews
sections.text: While a feature's Property panel is open, the model is rolled back to just before that feature and the feature is shown in colour: yellow for material it adds and red (seen through the body) for material it removes. Fillets and chamfers show the material they add or remove; reference geometry being edited is drawn in orange. Click ✔ (or Enter) to finish. Every value field accepts numbers or equations (see Equations in the Evaluate chapter).

sections.title: Extrude and Extrude Cut
sections.text: Profiles uses the same canvas selector as Loft. Click inside a closed region or on its contour to add it; click it again or use its remove button to deselect it. Select several coplanar profiles to extrude them together, including profiles from different sketches. Clicking a sketch in the tree selects its whole profile, including text and generated outlines. Picking an individual region afterwards replaces that whole-sketch selection. Nested regions can be selected separately, so you can extrude a ring or just the disk inside its hole. Model faces as profiles: click a flat face of the model (where no sketch profile is under the cursor) to use the face itself as a profile, holes and all, without drawing a sketch on it; click it again to remove it. A face profile lies in the face's plane and extrudes out of its body (tick Reverse direction to go into it, for a cut). It can be combined with sketch profiles in the same plane and takes every end condition, the draft and every operation; it cannot be a Thin Feature. If the face changes when earlier features change, the profile follows it. Chain selection selects connected curves. Turn it off to pick individual segments, then choose Add selected contour or press Enter; Escape clears the unfinished selection. Open contours enable Thin Feature. Turn off Select profiles in canvas to pick end references or target bodies; choosing an up-to end condition also switches to reference picking. Existing whole-sketch extrusions continue to build as before. Extrudes a sketch profile into a solid, or cuts it out. Start and End are independent. Start from → Profile plane preserves the usual extrusion. Offset from profile translates the starting plane by a signed distance along the first selected profile's normal; expressions are supported. Plane / planar face projects the profiles along the extrusion direction onto the underlying plane of the selected reference, including inclined planes. Use Pick start surface in canvas or the Start surface list. End references have their own picker and do not replace the start reference. Blind depth, symmetric and two-sided distances are measured from the new start. Reversing the extrusion changes its extent direction while preserving the start offset. With an inclined start and a distance end, both caps follow the starting plane, separated along the extrusion direction. Up To Surface, Offset From Surface and Up To Vertex retain independent end references. Crossing boundaries, zero thickness and a starting plane parallel to the extrusion direction are rejected. The options apply to solid extrusions, cuts, Thin Feature and selected profile regions; saved start-plane references follow source edits. Surface Extrude retains its existing start behavior. End conditions: End condition Meaning --- --- Blind A set depth Mid Plane The total depth split equally on both sides of the sketch Two sides Independent Depth and Second depth on opposite sides of the profile plane Through All / Through All – Both Through every body, in one or both directions Up To Vertex Click a model vertex or choose a reference point Up To Surface Click a flat model face or choose a plane; angled surfaces are supported and the extrusion is trimmed to the surface Offset From Surface As Up To Surface, at a set distance from it Second Side: with a one-sided end condition (Blind, Through All, Up To Vertex, Up To Surface or Offset From Surface), tick Second side to extrude the other way from the start as well, to an end of its own: Blind (its own Depth), Through All, Up To Vertex, Up To Surface or Offset From Surface, with its own vertex or surface picker (Pick second side surface in canvas). The second side always goes the opposite way to the first: an end of the second side that lies on the first side's side of the profile is refused. Both sides share the start, the operation and the Thin Feature; the draft is shared too (each side drafted away from the profile) unless Second side drafted on its own is ticked (see Draft). Mid Plane, Two sides and Through All – Both already reach both ways and do not offer it. Options: Operation: Join merges with existing material where possible; New body keeps the result separate; Cut removes material; Intersect keeps only the material inside the extrusion. A Join that does not touch existing material makes a new body. An Intersect changes each body the extrusion overlaps and leaves the others as they are; with Feature Scope limited to chosen bodies, a chosen body it does not overlap is removed. An Intersect that overlaps no body is refused, and an Intersect feature cannot be patterned or mirrored. Thin Feature: makes a wall of the given thickness from the profile; direction one side, other side or mid-plane. Open sketches switch it on automatically. Draft: tilts the walls by the Draft angle, about the plane the extrusion starts from: the solid narrows away from the profile, or widens with Draft outward. The walls of holes in the profile tilt the other way with them, so the material keeps one taper (a cut narrows as it goes in). Mid Plane, Two sides, Through All – Both and a second side draft each side away from the profile. Up To and Offset From an angled surface take the draft too: the walls tilt about the profile and the angled end is trimmed with them. From an angled start surface the walls tilt about the start surface, so the profile's outline is kept where the extrusion starts. If the walls would meet before the end, the draft is refused. With a second side, or with Two sides, Second side drafted on its own gives the second side (the Second depth) a Second side draft angle of its own, inward or (Second side drafted outward) outward; 0 leaves it straight. Feature Scope (cuts and intersects): All bodies by default; untick it and click the bodies to cut or intersect.
