Projected CurveProjects a sketch along its normal onto faces, as a 3D curve
Composite CurveJoins model edges end to end into one curve

Projected and composite curves can be used as sweep paths, lofted surface profiles, curve-driven pattern paths and boundary surface curves.

sections.title: Flatten Surface
sections.text: Click the faces to unroll. Faces that unroll (cylinders, cones, bent sheets) come out exact. A doubly curved face (for example a dome) can't lie flat without stretching: it is spread out keeping its edge lengths as well as possible, and the note gives the size, the area change and how much the edge lengths changed. Relaxing passes sets how hard it tries. A closed tube needs a seam (Split Line) to open out.
sections.html: Click the faces to unroll. Faces that unroll (cylinders, cones, bent sheets) come out exact. A doubly curved face (for example a dome) can't lie flat without stretching: it is spread out keeping its edge lengths as well as possible, and the note gives the size, the area change and how much the edge lengths changed. Relaxing passes sets how hard it tries. A closed tube needs a seam (Split Line) to open out.

sections.title: Meshes and closing surfaces
sections.text: Convert to Solid (also right-click a surface body): surface bodies that together enclose a volume, or a mesh, are joined (edges closer than the gap tolerance meet) and made into one solid. When they leave gaps it says how many open edges and holes there are. Repair Mesh: closes the holes of a surface body or a mesh with missing pieces (flat holes with a flat face, curved holes with a filling surface, holes in a mesh with triangles), turns triangles that face the wrong way round, and makes a solid. Option: the largest hole to close. Surface quality can be checked with Zebra Stripes, Curvature and Draft Analysis (Evaluate and Tools chapter).
sections.html:
• Convert to Solid (also right-click a surface body): surface bodies that together enclose a volume, or a mesh, are joined (edges closer than the gap tolerance meet) and made into one solid. When they leave gaps it says how many open edges and holes there are.
  • Repair Mesh: closes the holes of a surface body or a mesh with missing pieces (flat holes with a flat face, curved holes with a filling surface, holes in a mesh with triangles), turns triangles that face the wrong way round, and makes a solid. Option: the largest hole to close.

Surface quality can be checked with Zebra Stripes, Curvature and Draft Analysis (Evaluate and Tools chapter).

sections.title: Reference Plane
sections.text: Reference Plane, Reference Axis and Reference Point share a References and Relations panel with three numbered slots. Pick sketch geometry, model geometry or an earlier reference feature in the canvas or tree. The Choose reference geometry list also offers individual sketch lines, arcs, circles, supported splines and points (including the sketch origin), grouped by source sketch. Entries show the entity name and stable ID; suppressed, failed and later sketches are omitted. Hidden source sketches are temporarily displayed without changing their saved visibility. Click a slot to replace its reference; a fourth pick never discards an existing reference. Click a selected reference again, or its remove button, to remove it. References remain linked to their sources. Each slot offers compatible Relation choices. Automatic chooses the usual relation for the selected combination; selecting an explicit relation keeps that choice when other references change. Distances and angles accept expressions. References must precede the feature in the tree. The displayed rectangle of a reference plane is centered near its defining line, point or path location, projected onto the plane. This display position does not change the plane's sketch coordinate system. For rotation about a line, use Coincident / through on the line and At angle on a reference plane. Fully Defined means the supported constraints have a finite solution with no remaining continuous freedom. Under Defined identifies missing constraints; Conflicting identifies incompatible geometry, relations or values. An axis direction alone does not fix its position, and two points alone do not fix a plane. Incomplete and conflicting definitions cannot be accepted. When two distinct geometric solutions exist, Solution 1 / Solution 2 selects the branch; opposite normals of the same plane are handled by Reverse its normal instead. Reference geometry Available plane relations and constructions --- --- Planar face or plane Coincident, Offset, Parallel, Perpendicular, At angle Point or vertex Coincident / through Straight edge, sketch line or reference axis Coincident / through, Parallel, Perpendicular, At angle; Normal at position Sketch circle/arc or circular model edge Its containing plane supplies Coincident, Parallel, Perpendicular and At angle relations Two planes/faces with Midplane relations Midplane of parallel planes, or either angular bisector Cylindrical face Tangent, with an angle round the cylinder; optionally parallel to one selected plane, with either side available Examples: three non-collinear points define a plane; a line with Coincident plus an external point defines the plane through both; a line with Perpendicular plus a point defines a normal plane through that point. A line with Coincident and a plane with At angle can define two angular solutions. Skew lines, inconsistent angles and invalid tangent combinations report conflicts. Normal at position uses the selected segment's start, midpoint, end or a distance within a straight segment. A reference axis supplies a direction and its stored anchor. The solver uses affine equations and the unit-normal constraint, rather than a tessellated approximation. Numerical rank and consistency checks distinguish free, unique and incompatible definitions. Tangency currently supports a cylinder alone or a cylinder with one parallel plane; midplane supports two plane references. Arbitrary curved-surface relations and additional constraints on these special constructions are not supported yet. Placement transforms the constructed plane after its reference relations have been solved: move along its normal, turn its sketch axes in the plane, or reverse its normal. An Offset relation already supplies its signed distance and has Flip offset direction. Existing plane and axis constructions keep their original geometry and anchor when opened for editing. The panel identifies the preserved construction; changing a reference or relation upgrades it to the constraint definition. Cancel restores the original saved definition.
sections.html:
Reference Plane, Reference Axis and Reference Point share a References and Relations panel with three numbered slots. Pick sketch geometry, model geometry or an earlier reference feature in the canvas or tree. The Choose reference geometry list also offers individual sketch lines, arcs, circles, supported splines and points (including the sketch origin), grouped by source sketch. Entries show the entity name and stable ID; suppressed, failed and later sketches are omitted. Hidden source sketches are temporarily displayed without changing their saved visibility. Click a slot to replace its reference; a fourth pick never discards an existing reference. Click a selected reference again, or its remove button, to remove it. References remain linked to their sources.

Each slot offers compatible Relation choices. Automatic chooses the usual relation for the selected combination; selecting an explicit relation keeps that choice when other references change. Distances and angles accept expressions. References must precede the feature in the tree.

The displayed rectangle of a reference plane is centered near its defining line, point or path location, projected onto the plane. This display position does not change the plane's sketch coordinate system. For rotation about a line, use Coincident / through on the line and At angle on a reference plane.

Fully Defined means the supported constraints have a finite solution with no remaining continuous freedom. Under Defined identifies missing constraints; Conflicting identifies incompatible geometry, relations or values. An axis direction alone does not fix its position, and two points alone do not fix a plane. Incomplete and conflicting definitions cannot be accepted. When two distinct geometric solutions exist, Solution 1 / Solution 2 selects the branch; opposite normals of the same plane are handled by Reverse its normal instead.

Reference geometryAvailable plane relations and constructions
Planar face or planeCoincident, Offset, Parallel, Perpendicular, At angle
Point or vertexCoincident / through
Straight edge, sketch line or reference axisCoincident / through, Parallel, Perpendicular, At angle; Normal at position
Sketch circle/arc or circular model edgeIts containing plane supplies Coincident, Parallel, Perpendicular and At angle relations
Two planes/faces with Midplane relationsMidplane of parallel planes, or either angular bisector
Cylindrical faceTangent, with an angle round the cylinder; optionally parallel to one selected plane, with either side available

Examples: three non-collinear points define a plane; a line with Coincident plus an external point defines the plane through both; a line with Perpendicular plus a point defines a normal plane through that point. A line with Coincident and a plane with At angle can define two angular solutions. Skew lines, inconsistent angles and invalid tangent combinations report conflicts. Normal at position uses the selected segment's start, midpoint, end or a distance within a straight segment. A reference axis supplies a direction and its stored anchor.

The solver uses affine equations and the unit-normal constraint, rather than a tessellated approximation. Numerical rank and consistency checks distinguish free, unique and incompatible definitions. Tangency currently supports a cylinder alone or a cylinder with one parallel plane; midplane supports two plane references. Arbitrary curved-surface relations and additional constraints on these special constructions are not supported yet.

Placement transforms the constructed plane after its reference relations have been solved: move along its normal, turn its sketch axes in the plane, or reverse its normal. An Offset relation already supplies its signed distance and has Flip offset direction.

Existing plane and axis constructions keep their original geometry and anchor when opened for editing. The panel identifies the preserved construction; changing a reference or relation upgrades it to the constraint definition. Cancel restores the original saved definition.

sections.title: Plane Along Path and point along a curve
sections.text: In Reference Plane or Reference Point, select a sketch line, arc, circle or spline, a model edge, or an earlier helix/3D/composite/projected curve feature. Choose the reference relation Along path (arc length). The source picker and tree also offer curve features; a feature containing several disconnected routes must be reduced to one connected path first. Position offers Distance along curve, Fraction (0–1), Start, Half arc length and End. Distances and fractions accept expressions. Reverse path direction measures from the opposite end and reverses the tangent used by the plane. A fraction follows changes in the total curve length; a distance retains its physical length when the source changes. Closed paths retain the curve's existing seam; distances outside the path are rejected rather than wrapped. The plane passes through the computed position, has its origin there and is normal to the local tangent. The point uses that same position. A point can lie at a corner or cusp; a plane cannot be made there without a unique tangent. The preview identifies a conflict at detected corners, singularities or nonsmooth closed seams instead of choosing one tangent arbitrarily. Locations use adaptive integration of curve speed and bounded inversion of the resulting arc length, independently of display tessellation. Sketch splines retain their original Bézier pieces, degree and rational weights. Model edges and curve features use derivatives of the actual CAD curve and an independent CAD length check. Position inversion targets 0.0000001 mm or 1e-10 of the path length, whichever is larger; refinement exhaustion reports an error. These are numerical convergence controls, not a certified global error bound. Existing Midpoint and straight-segment Distance relations keep their previous meanings; choose Along path explicitly for arc-length placement.

sections.title: Reference Axis
sections.text: Uses the same three slots, per-reference relations and definition states. Two points define a through-axis; two intersecting planes define an axis in both. A straight edge or sketch line supplies its line, a circular edge supplies its centre axis, and a cylindrical or conical face supplies its centre axis. Plane Perpendicular plus a point defines a normal axis through that point. Parallel and perpendicular relations can constrain the direction while other references constrain the position. Axes remain linked, are drawn dashed and can drive a revolve or a pattern. Right-click an edge and choose Reference Axis to preselect it. Parallel distinct planes, coincident points and zero-length directions cannot define the requested axis.

sections.title: Reference Point
sections.text: Choose Coordinates (expressions allowed) or Reference geometry. The latter uses the shared slots and states. A point/vertex can be copied; a selected sketch line or model edge can supply its start, end or midpoint, and a circular curve can supply its centre. Distance from start currently supports straight segments and rejects distances outside the segment. Coincident relations intersect straight lines and planes: two crossing lines, a line crossing a plane, or three independent planes can define one point. A point on one plane retains two degrees of freedom; one on a line retains one. Skew lines, incompatible planes and missing references report conflicts. Circular and other curved-edge midpoint positions use the kernel's normalized curve parameter, preserving the existing Edge midpoint behavior; they are not a general arc-length locator. Use Along path (arc length) above to locate a point by physical curve distance or fraction. Two references where one is curved also give a point where they meet: a curved model edge (circle, arc, spline) and a plane, a flat face, a curved face or another edge, or a curved face and an axis. When they meet more than once, the panel says how many crossings there are and Next solution steps through them, in a fixed order. A curved face and a plane meet along a curve, so that pair is refused: pick an edge of the face instead. Right-click a vertex and choose Reference Point to preselect it. Coordinate mode retains its stored reference choices but does not depend on or evaluate them.

sections.title: Editing features
sections.text: Double-click a feature, or right-click ▸ Edit Feature, to open its Property panel. Select a feature and press Del (or Edit ▸ Delete) to delete it. Edit ▸ Undo / Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) works on the whole part history. Rebuild (Ctrl+B, or the quick button) rebuilds the part. A feature that fails shows an error in the tree so you can fix or re-pick its references (see Fix References).
sections.html:
• Double-click a feature, or right-click ▸ Edit Feature, to open its Property panel.
  • Select a feature and press Del (or Edit ▸ Delete) to delete it.
  • Edit ▸ Undo / Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) works on the whole part history.
  • Rebuild (Ctrl+B, or the quick button) rebuilds the part.
  • A feature that fails shows an error in the tree so you can fix or re-pick its references (see Fix References).

sections.title: References that follow edits
sections.text: Features that use picked edges and faces (fillets, chamfers, shells, drafts, axes…) find them again after the model changes. An edge remembers the faces on its two sides and whether it is an outside or inside corner. When a dimension moves it so far that other edges now lie nearer its old place, the right edge is still found, and an edge of another kind is not taken for it. A face that moved is found as the face facing the same way that is clearly nearest. A reference found again this way is updated, so it keeps following the model.

sections.title: Fix References
sections.text: Tools ▸ Fix References… lists every feature that failed to rebuild, what went wrong and which of its edges or faces are no longer in the model. Open it also by clicking the red error count in the status bar, or by right-clicking a failed feature. For each feature: Button What it does --- --- Edit Opens the feature (or sketch) to pick its references again Remove missing Keeps the references that are still found and drops the others Suppress Leaves the feature out for now Fix them from the top: a feature can fail only because one above it did. The list follows every rebuild while it is open.

sections.title: Rollback bar
sections.text: The blue line at the bottom of the tree. Drag it up, or right-click a feature ▸ Roll Back / Roll to End. Features below the bar are suppressed, and new features are inserted above it.
sections.html: The blue line at the bottom of the tree. Drag it up, or right-click a feature ▸ Roll Back / Roll to End. Features below the bar are suppressed, and new features are inserted above it.

sections.title: Reordering features
sections.text: Drag a feature up or down the tree. Its absorbed sketch moves with it. A move that would break a reference is refused with the reason.
sections.html: Drag a feature up or down the tree. Its absorbed sketch moves with it. A move that would break a reference is refused with the reason.

sections.title: Reference arrows
sections.text: Select a feature in the tree. Blue arrows come from what it uses; purple arrows go to what uses it.

sections.title: Base Flange
sections.text: A closed sketch (holes allowed) becomes a sheet of the given thickness. The bend radius and K-factor set here become the part's defaults. Bend calculation (Base Flange, Sheet Metal Extrude, Lofted Bend, Transition): K-factor, or, from your bend table for this thickness and radius, the Bend allowance (the length a 90° bend takes flat) or the Bend deduction (how much shorter the flat is than the two outside lengths to the sharp, for a 90° bend). RazorCAD works out the K-factor it gives (refused when outside 0 to 1), so every flat length agrees with the table at 90° and other angles follow in proportion. Bend table (by angle) takes the allowance for several angles ("30: 1.5; 45: 2.0; 90: 4.2", for this thickness and the default radius): each bend's allowance is read from it, straight between its rows and in proportion past its ends; bends of another radius use the K-factor its 90° allowance gives.

sections.title: Gauge tables
sections.text: Base Flange, Sheet Metal Extrude and Transition / Reducer have a Gauge list: mild steel, steel gauges, stainless 304, and aluminium 5052 and 6061-T6. Picking a gauge sets the thickness, inside bend radius and K-factor. Save… keeps your own values as a gauge.

sections.title: Sheet Metal Extrude
sections.text: Extrudes an open sketch of lines and arcs into a sheet metal part. Arcs in the sketch are bends of their own radius; sharp corners get a bend of the inside radius set in the panel. Material goes on one side, the other side or both sides of the sketch; depth one way, reversed or mid-plane. A circle on its own is rolled into a cylinder, leaving a seam gap. Flanges, hems, Flatten and DXF export work on it.

Material goes on one side, the other side or both sides of the sketch; depth one way, reversed or mid-plane. A circle on its own is rolled into a cylinder, leaving a seam gap. sections.title: Lofted Bend
sections.text: A sheet metal part between two open profile sketches (each one chain of lines and arcs), for example a round-to-square transition, hopper or duct piece. Points are matched along both profiles by length, keeping every corner of either profile. Method: Bent makes flat facets folded along straight lines, each fold a bend line in the flat pattern and DXF; set the number of divisions. Formed makes a smooth sheet (rolled or pressed), with the set number of forming lines along the profiles. The flat pattern is developed at the neutral layer (K-factor) and works with Flatten, DXF export and flat pattern drawings. Material on the other side flips the thickness. A cut through a lofted bend is carried into its flat pattern, and the cut edges are square to the sheet, as a laser-cut blank formed to shape would be. This makes trimmed conical parts possible: loft the cone between two arcs, then cut it to the outline with a revolved cut. Edge flanges, corner reliefs and closed corners can't be added to a lofted bend; its shape comes from the profiles.
sections.html:
A sheet metal part between two open profile sketches (each one chain of lines and arcs), for example a round-to-square transition, hopper or duct piece. Points are matched along both profiles by length, keeping every corner of either profile.

sections.title: Transition / Reducer
sections.text: Cones, concentric and eccentric reducers, square-, rectangle-, triangle-, pentagon- and hexagon-to-round transitions (either way up) and polygon frustums. Sizes, offset and rotation are set in the panel; sizes can be inside, outside or mean. A sketch line from bottom centre to top centre places the part and sets its height; change the line and the part follows. Started with no sketch, it asks for a plane and opens the Line tool. The part is made from a number of equal pieces, each a sheet metal body with its own flat pattern: a cone from one piece or more, a flat-sided transition from two or more, with seams at the middle of the flat sides or at the corners. Formed (rolled, with a set number of forming lines per corner or round the whole part) or bent (bump formed with a set number of bends).

Closed corners keep a gap (default 0.5 mm). For Overlap, Swap reverses which covers, and the Bend region is a V cutout or Closed.

sections.title: Miter Flange
sections.text: A flange with a profile of up to four segments along a chain of edges. Each segment has a length (to the outside of the bends) and an angle; a negative angle folds back the other way, so 90 / 90 makes a C and 90 / −90 a Z. The corners are mitred (closed, with a gap) at every level. First bend sets where the material sits on the edge, as for an edge flange.

sections.title: Sketched Bend
sections.text: Draw lines on the top or bottom face of a flat part of the sheet; the sheet is bent along each one. Set the angle, the radius (or the part's), whether the bend is centred on the line or starts or ends at it, the fold direction and which side stays put. The flat pattern stays the plate it was.

sections.title: Jog
sections.text: One sketch line on a face makes two opposite bends that step the sheet over by a height. The height is measured face to face, outside to outside or inside to inside; the jog says when the height is too small for the bends.
sections.html: One sketch line on a face makes two opposite bends that step the sheet over by a height. The height is measured face to face, outside to outside or inside to inside; the jog says when the height is too small for the bends.

sections.title: Cross Break
sections.text: Click flat faces to mark an X of shallow stiffening folds. It shows in Flatten, in the DXF (on the Forming marks layer, with a note) and in flat pattern drawings.
sections.html: Click flat faces to mark an X of shallow stiffening folds. It shows in Flatten, in the DXF (on the Forming marks layer, with a note) and in flat pattern drawings.

sections.title: Tab and Slot
sections.text: Click the edge of one sheet metal part where it sits on another, then the face of the other part. Tabs are added along the edge and matching slots, with clearance all round, are cut through the other part, so the parts locate each other for welding. Settings: number of tabs, tab length, tab height (empty: through the other part), margin at each end (empty: evenly spread) and clearance. Both flat patterns and DXFs get the tabs and slots.

sections.title: Forming Tools
sections.text: Forming Tools presses a form into the sheet. Place forms at clicked points, or exactly at the points and circle centres of a sketch on the face (for a louver, its lines). They are pressed toward the face they are placed on, or the other way. Form Settings --- --- Dimple Diameter, depth Extruded (flanged) hole Hole diameter inside the collar, collar height, bend radius Louver Width back from the slit, opening height, hood side; drawn as a line on the face (the slit) Bead A round-topped stiffening rib along each sketch line, its width and height (at most half its width), its ends rounded Lance A bridge: slits along the sketch line and its width from it, the strip between pressed out by the height and ramped back at 45° at its ends; both slits are cut lines in the flat pattern Emboss Each closed outline of the sketch raised (or pressed, with Flip) by the height, with straight walls the sheet's thickness; its outline is marked in the flat pattern The flat pattern gets a centre mark and a note for each form, an extruded hole's pre-hole (the collar laid flat) and a louver's slit as a cut. Forms stay with the part through later sheet metal features and are left off, rather than breaking the part, if one can't be made.

LanceA bridge: slits along the sketch line and its width from it, the strip between pressed out by the height and ramped back at 45° at its ends; both slits are cut lines in the flat pattern
EmbossEach closed outline of the sketch raised (or pressed, with Flip) by the height, with straight walls the sheet's thickness; its outline is marked in the flat pattern

The flat pattern gets a centre mark and a note for each form, an extruded hole's pre-hole (the collar laid flat) and a louver's slit as a cut. Forms stay with the part through later sheet metal features and are left off, rather than breaking the part, if one can't be made.

sections.title: Gusset
sections.text: Click a bend (its round face) to press a stiffening dart across it at that point. Set the size of each leg from the inside corner and the width across the bend; tick Pressed down to press it the other way. The flat pattern marks it. (For gusset plates between structural members, see the Fast Structure chapter.)
sections.html: Click a bend (its round face) to press a stiffening dart across it at that point. Set the size of each leg from the inside corner and the width across the bend; tick Pressed down to press it the other way. The flat pattern marks it. (For gusset plates between structural members, see the Fast Structure chapter.)

sections.title: Corner Relief
sections.text: Adds a rectangular, circular or tear relief at every corner where two bends meet.
sections.html: Adds a rectangular, circular or tear relief at every corner where two bends meet.

sections.title: Closed Corner
sections.text: Closes the corners between 90° flanges: one flange covers the other's end, with a gap. Corner type: Overlap, Underlap, Butt (square ends: each flange runs on up to the other's inside face, the gap between their inside edges, the bends in a V cutout) or Mitre (the gap across the mitre, bends included). Which corners: click a face of a flange next to a corner and the matching flange is found automatically; the clicked flange is the one that overlaps or tucks under. With no corners picked, every corner of the body is closed. Swap reverses which flange covers. Bend region: V cutout (default) runs each bend into the corner as it would form from the flat, leaving a small teardrop-shaped opening with a relief at the corner point. Closed keeps the bends meeting on the diagonal. The flat pattern matches the folded part at closed corners, including each bend's run-on, the relief and the corner round.
sections.html:
Closes the corners between 90° flanges: one flange covers the other's end, with a gap.

sections.title: Unbend and Bend
sections.text: Unbend keeps the picked face in place and flattens the rest. Features after it (such as cuts across bends) are made in the flat. Bend folds it back to where it was. Both appear in the tree.
sections.html: Unbend keeps the picked face in place and flattens the rest. Features after it (such as cuts across bends) are made in the flat. Bend folds it back to where it was. Both appear in the tree.

sections.title: Cuts and other features on sheet metal
sections.text: Cuts on sheet metal (extruded cut and so on) become holes in the flat pattern, so the flat pattern always matches. Holes (the Hole feature) work on sheet metal too. Other features that change a sheet metal body are allowed, but the flat pattern can't follow them; this is shown in Body Properties and the DXF preview.

Other features that change a sheet metal body are allowed, but the flat pattern can't follow them; this is shown in Body Properties and the DXF preview.

sections.title: Flatten
sections.text: Click Flatten on the tab, or right-click the body ▸ View Flat Pattern. The flat pattern is shown on its own; Esc or Flatten again restores the view as it was. While it is shown, Export DXF… on the flat pattern banner (or right-click the view) exports it straight away.
sections.html: Click Flatten on the tab, or right-click the body ▸ View Flat Pattern. The flat pattern is shown on its own; Esc or Flatten again restores the view as it was. While it is shown, Export DXF… on the flat pattern banner (or right-click the view) exports it straight away.

sections.title: Convert to Sheet Metal
sections.text: Turns an ordinary body into sheet metal. Pick a flat face of a thin-walled body (for example a STEP export of a sheet metal part, or a shelled box), or of a knitted surface of flat faces (enter the thickness). RazorCAD follows that side of the sheet across every smooth edge, through flat faces and cylindrical bend faces, so the whole body is found. Each bend keeps its own radius and angle. Bends that run straight into each other with no flat between (rolled shapes such as a fan scroll) are joined automatically. Cut-outs in bends are kept and holes stay true circles in the DXF. Sharp-cornered bodies (shelled boxes) get bends of the chosen radius at every edge between two flat faces. A flange whose ends run right up against the material beside it, with no relief (a flange off a cross bar between the sides of a window, or off the edges of a slot), is ripped there: the flat pattern (and its DXF) has a cut line along each flange end, across the bend and on to the flange's edge, on the cut-outs layer, as the part is cut and bent. The panel shows what was found in the body, for example "thickness 3 mm · bend radii R300, R227, R13 (inside, 3 bends)" or "4 sharp edges". Use the body's thickness and Use the body's bend radii are on by default. Untick either to set your own value (pre-filled with the detected one). A body curved other than in plain bends (a square-to-round transition or a reducer from another program, a cone) is unrolled: laid out flat at the neutral layer, triangle by triangle, so its flat pattern keeps every length; a ring is cut open at a seam. For a cone, click its curved face. A closed tube (bends all the way round) is unrolled the same way, cut open at a seam. A face curved both ways (a dished end, a spherical cap) can't be laid flat exactly: it is spread out as nearly as it can be (from its middle out along its profile, then relaxed so its lengths change as little as they can), and scaled to the dish's own area (pressed, the sheet keeps its volume). The note gives how far it stretches (the most over 98 % of it, and on average): use it as a blank size to press from, and check it against a trial. Cuts in such a sheet are unrolled with it (the hole is in the flat pattern); flanges, hems and corners can't be added (as on a lofted bend). A body that RazorCAD folded itself (for example its STEP export) gets its closed corners back as RazorCAD made them: the corner type (V cutout, closed mitre or butt), which flange covers which and the gap are worked out from the body, and the relief and curved V lines are made again exactly. Other corners are traced from the body as they are. After converting, the sheet's volume is compared with the body's. The feature note warns when they differ by more than 0.5 % (for example a nut or motor part that isn't sheet metal). A curved surface that is curved one way only (a cylinder, or a profile swept straight) is converted into a rolled sheet: its section is followed by smoothly joined arcs, each a bend of its own radius. Arc fit tolerance (default 0.05 mm) sets how closely it follows the surface. Thickness goes behind the surface, in front of it, or both sides. Trim where the sheet would run into itself (on by default) trims a rolled sheet back where its two ends would meet, leaving a small clearance.

sections.title: Etch Lines
sections.text: Sheet Metal ▸ Etch Lines: pick a sketch drawn on the top or bottom face of a flat part of the sheet. Its lines, arcs, circles, splines and text are marked in the flat pattern, for etching, scribing or marking part numbers and bend marks. They go on the DXF's ETCH layer (DXF Settings can leave them out) and show in flat-pattern drawing views (View Properties ▸ Etch lines), clipped to the face they are on. The folded part is not changed; the etch lines show on the model as thin lines.
sections.html: Sheet Metal ▸ Etch Lines: pick a sketch drawn on the top or bottom face of a flat part of the sheet. Its lines, arcs, circles, splines and text are marked in the flat pattern, for etching, scribing or marking part numbers and bend marks. They go on the DXF's ETCH layer (DXF Settings can leave them out) and show in flat-pattern drawing views (View Properties ▸ Etch lines), clipped to the face they are on. The folded part is not changed; the etch lines show on the model as thin lines.

sections.title: Sheet Metal Check
sections.text: Sheet Metal Check lists every bend of the sheet metal body: direction, angle, inside radius, length and the straight flange on each side. It warns about flanges shorter than 3 × thickness past their bend, and holes closer than 2 × thickness + radius to a bend.
sections.html: Sheet Metal Check lists every bend of the sheet metal body: direction, angle, inside radius, length and the straight flange on each side. It warns about flanges shorter than 3 × thickness past their bend, and holes closer than 2 × thickness + radius to a bend.

sections.title: Sheet metal Body Properties
sections.text: Body Properties for a sheet metal body shows thickness, bend radius and K-factor, number of bends, overall flat size, flat area, mass and quantity, plus: Cut length: the total length of the flat outline plus every hole and cut-out, and the number of pierces (closed contours), for laser-cutting estimates. Also shown in the DXF part information and under flat pattern drawing views. Flat pattern seen from: top face or bottom face. The bottom face mirrors the pattern and swaps UP / DOWN bend lines and notes. Flatten, DXF export and drawing views all follow it.
sections.html:
Body Properties for a sheet metal body shows thickness, bend radius and K-factor, number of bends, overall flat size, flat area, mass and quantity, plus:

  • Cut length: the total length of the flat outline plus every hole and cut-out, and the number of pierces (closed contours), for laser-cutting estimates. Also shown in the DXF part information and under flat pattern drawing views.
  • Flat pattern seen from: top face or bottom face. The bottom face mirrors the pattern and swaps UP / DOWN bend lines and notes. Flatten, DXF export and drawing views all follow it.

sections.title: Exporting flat patterns as DXF
sections.text: Right-click a sheet metal body (tree or view) ▸ Export Flat Pattern as DXF, or Export DXF on the tab. Export All DXF: choose a target folder; one file per body, named after the body. Identical bodies give one file with the quantity multiplied by the count. Nest Flat Patterns : lays every sheet metal body's flat pattern out on stock sheets (width × height, a margin round the sheet, a gap between parts, parts turned 90° where that fits better). Identical bodies are counted, times each body's quantity and the number of Sets. Parts are placed by their true outlines (the default: bottom left first, the biggest first, into each other's gaps and inside the holes of others) or by the rectangles round them (fast). They can be turned not at all, by 90° steps, or (by outlines) by 45° or 15° steps. The result shows each sheet and how much of it is used; Export DXF… writes one DXF with the sheets side by side, their outlines on layer SHEET and each part's outline and holes, named at its middle. Each file is shown in a preview window with its layer colours and line types, which can be changed there. Buttons: Export, Skip This One and Abort Export. In the preview, zoom with the wheel, pan by dragging and double-click or Fit to see it all. Click lines to select them (Ctrl or Shift adds, Shift+drag for a box, Ctrl+A for all), then Delete them, give them their own Line type, or move them to another Layer (for example make a line an etch line). Undo and Restore All put them back. These edits apply to that one export. Options: bend lines, bend notes, bend region (hidden) lines, etch lines and part information.

sections.title: DXF Settings
sections.text: DXF Settings on the Sheet Metal tab sets the defaults for every export: layer mapping (colours and line types) and options. Defaults: up bends red, down bends blue, etch lines yellow dashed. Reset to Defaults restores them.
sections.html: DXF Settings on the Sheet Metal tab sets the defaults for every export: layer mapping (colours and line types) and options. Defaults: up bends red, down bends blue, etch lines yellow dashed. Reset to Defaults restores them.

sections.title: Fast Structure
sections.text: The Fast Structure tab builds welded frames (weldments) from standard steel profiles: Structural Member, Trim/Extend, End Cap, Gusset, Weld Bead and Cut List. It also has a 3D Sketch button, since frames are often laid out in 3D.
sections.html: The Fast Structure tab builds welded frames (weldments) from standard steel profiles: Structural Member, Trim/Extend, End Cap, Gusset, Weld Bead and Cut List. It also has a 3D Sketch button, since frames are often laid out in 3D.

sections.title: Structural Member
sections.text: Pick a profile and a sketch or 3D sketch: every line and arc of it becomes a member, each its own body named after its profile. Add more sketches to the Path list for a frame in 3D, for example the top of a table and its legs; the joints between them are treated too. Arcs, and the bends of a 3D sketch with a bend radius, become bent members. Profile Types --- --- Hollow sections Square (SHS), rectangular (RHS), circular (CHS / pipe) Angles Equal and unequal angle Channels and beams Channel (PFC / UPN); I-beam (UB, UC, IPE, HEA) Bars Flat bar, round bar Sizes come from AS/NZS or EN/ISO tables, or enter your own dimensions. Corners where two members meet end to end: Mitre, Butt (first or second member trimmed) or None (members meet at the sketch points). Trimmed ends: square cut on the face, or coped to the other member's outside. A member ending on the middle of another (a T-joint), or under a corner (a table leg), is trimmed to it, square on its face. Pipes and round bars are always coped (fish-mouthed). Alignment: which point of the profile the sketch line runs through (centre, corners or edges), a profile rotation, and mirror.
sections.html:

Add more sketches to the Path list for a frame in 3D, for example the top of a table and its legs; the joints between them are treated too. Arcs, and the bends of a 3D sketch with a bend radius, become bent members.

ProfileTypes

BarsFlat bar, round bar

Sizes come from AS/NZS or EN/ISO tables, or enter your own dimensions.

  • Corners where two members meet end to end: Mitre, Butt (first or second member trimmed) or None (members meet at the sketch points). Trimmed ends: square cut on the face, or coped to the other member's outside.
  • A member ending on the middle of another (a T-joint), or under a corner (a table leg), is trimmed to it, square on its face. Pipes and round bars are always coped (fish-mouthed).
  • Alignment: which point of the profile the sketch line runs through (centre, corners or edges), a profile rotation, and mirror.

sections.title: Trim/Extend
sections.text: Click the members to trim on the model, then the boundary: a plane or another body. Each member is trimmed (or, with Extend members that stop short of it, extended) at its end nearer the boundary, either cut square on the boundary's face or coped to the boundary body.
sections.html: Click the members to trim on the model, then the boundary: a plane or another body. Each member is trimmed (or, with Extend members that stop short of it, extended) at its end nearer the boundary, either cut square on the boundary's face or coped to the boundary body.

sections.title: End Cap
sections.text: Click the open end faces of tubes or pipes. A plate of the set thickness is added on the end (outside) or in the end (flush).
sections.html: Click the open end faces of tubes or pipes. A plate of the set thickness is added on the end (outside) or in the end (flush).

sections.title: Gusset
sections.text: Click two flat faces that meet at a corner, one on each member. A triangular plate fills the corner. Set the two leg lengths, the thickness, a corner chamfer for weld clearance, and where the plate sits along the corner (centred or to one side, plus an offset). End caps and gussets are bodies of their own, named by size for the cut list.
sections.html:
Click two flat faces that meet at a corner, one on each member. A triangular plate fills the corner. Set the two leg lengths, the thickness, a corner chamfer for weld clearance, and where the plate sits along the corner (centred or to one side, plus an offset).

End caps and gussets are bodies of their own, named by size for the cut list.

sections.title: Weld Bead
sections.text: Set the weld size and click the bodies to weld (none: every weldment member). A bead runs along every line where two of them touch; each joint is its own bead body.
sections.html: Set the weld size and click the bodies to weld (none: every weldment member). A bead runs along every line where two of them touch; each joint is its own bead body.

sections.title: Cut List
sections.text: Cut List lists identical members together, with their profile, length, end angles, quantity, total length and mass (from the bodies' materials), then plates and welds (with the total weld length). It also gives the total length of each profile. Export CSV… saves it for a spreadsheet. A drawing can show it as a Cut List Table (Drawings chapter).
sections.html: Cut List lists identical members together, with their profile, length, end angles, quantity, total length and mass (from the bodies' materials), then plates and welds (with the total weld length). It also gives the total length of each profile. Export CSV… saves it for a spreadsheet. A drawing can show it as a Cut List Table (Drawings chapter).

sections.title: Duct Fitting
sections.text: Duct Fitting (Weldments tab) makes a sheet metal duct fitting of outside sizes and a sheet thickness: a segmented elbow (angle, centre line radius, number of gores: two end gores and the rest full ones), a cone (reducer: the other diameter and the length), a round to rectangle transition, an offset (two parallel round ends side by side) or a lateral (a branch joining a main duct at an angle). Each is a body at the origin (move it with Move Body). Its flat patterns are developed on the middle of the sheet, with a seam allowance along the long seam: the message lists them and their sizes, and File ▸ Export ▸ Duct Patterns (DXF)… writes every fitting's patterns side by side, named with their quantities. Elbow gores are worked out exactly; transitions and offsets are unfolded by triangles, every edge at its true length.
sections.html: Duct Fitting (Weldments tab) makes a sheet metal duct fitting of outside sizes and a sheet thickness: a segmented elbow (angle, centre line radius, number of gores: two end gores and the rest full ones), a cone (reducer: the other diameter and the length), a round to rectangle transition, an offset (two parallel round ends side by side) or a lateral (a branch joining a main duct at an angle). Each is a body at the origin (move it with Move Body). Its flat patterns are developed on the middle of the sheet, with a seam allowance along the long seam: the message lists them and their sizes, and File ▸ Export ▸ Duct Patterns (DXF)… writes every fitting's patterns side by side, named with their quantities. Elbow gores are worked out exactly; transitions and offsets are unfolded by triangles, every edge at its true length.

sections.title: Pipe Route and Cable
sections.text: Pipe Route runs a pipe along the straight lines of a sketch or 3D sketch. Where a line branches square off a straight run, an equal tee goes in (ASME B16.9 sizes); other branches and crosses are reported. Choose a size (DN15 to DN300, Schedule 40 walls) or a tube of your own outside diameter and wall. Corners: Elbows puts a long radius elbow at each corner (1.5 × the nominal size, or the Bend radius you give), each elbow a body of its own; Bends makes one bent tube (3 × its diameter, or your radius). Reducer puts a concentric reducer (to a smaller size, its B16.9 length) at the first end, the last end (in the order the lines were drawn) or both. Flanges at the (other) ends adds a flange ring at each open end without a reducer. The straight pipes are weldment members, so the Cut List gives their lengths; the message sums them up. A line too short for the elbows at its ends is reported. Spool Drawing (Weldments tab, in a part with a pipe route) makes a drawing with one isometric view of the pipework, the cut list of the straight pipes and a FITTINGS table (each elbow, tee, reducer and flange, and how many). Cable sweeps a round cable or bundle along a sketch or 3D sketch (a 3D sketch spline through the points it must pass follows them smoothly). Give its Diameter, or the number of Wires and their diameter (the bundle is about 1.15 × d × √n across). The message gives the route length and the cut length with the Slack added. Harness Formboard lays the part's cables flat at their cut lengths, joined where their ends meet: each cable straight on from the one before it, branches fanned out at 45° steps. It shows the board with each cable's name and length and the points where cables meet, and Export DXF… writes it to lay out the board full size.

sections.title: Designing for 3D Printing
sections.text: The 3D Print tab has what a part made on a 3D printer needs: features that add a nut pocket or a printable hole in a click or two, a check of the part against what the printer can do, and an export laid out on the printer's bed. Every size it uses comes from the part's print profile: a printer and a material. Its buttons run left to right in the order you work: set up (profile, orientation), add features, check, export.
sections.html:
The 3D Print tab has what a part made on a 3D printer needs: features that add a nut pocket or a printable hole in a click or two, a check of the part against what the printer can do, and an export laid out on the printer's bed. Every size it uses comes from the part's print profile: a printer and a material.

Its buttons run left to right in the order you work: set up (profile, orientation), add features, check, export.

sections.title: Print Profile
sections.text: 3D Print ▸ Print Profile picks the profile this part uses and edits your own. A profile holds: Setting What it sets --- --- Bed X × Y × Z The printer's build volume: the bed check, Show Bed, Split for Printing Nozzle diameter, extrusion width, layer height The smallest walls (2 extrusion widths), the bridging steps Overhang limit How steep a face may face down, from vertical, without support (45° on FDM printers) Longest bridge The widest ceiling the printer can bridge Hole clearance Added each side to nut pockets Fits: press, snug, sliding, loose The gaps Fit Clearance uses (0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5 mm to start) Density, filament diameter The mass and filament length in the check Smallest hole, pin and gap The small-feature checks The material shrinks A warning about warping on long bases (ABS, ASA, nylon) Four profiles come with RazorCAD: PLA, PETG and ABS on a 0.4 mm nozzle, and a resin printer. They can't be changed: Copy… one and change the copy. Use for this part keeps the choice with the part (a copy of the profile is saved in the part file too); Make default is the profile for parts that have none. A change to one of your profiles applies to every part that uses it. Printer sets the bed from a list of popular printers (Prusa MK4 / MK4S, CORE One, CORE One L, XL and MINI+; Bambu Lab A1 mini, A1, P1S, X1C and H2D; Creality Ender-3 V3 and K1 Max; Elegoo Neptune 4 Pro; Anycubic Kobra 3). Chosen on a starting profile, it makes a copy of it for that printer, used for this part. The Prusa sizes are from Prusa's own pages; the others are from retailers' and reviewers' listings, and the dialog says so when one is chosen: check them against your printer's specifications. Typing a bed size of your own clears the printer. Slicer program (Windows app): Choose slicer program… picks the program Open in Slicer starts.
sections.html:
3D Print ▸ Print Profile picks the profile this part uses and edits your own. A profile holds:

SettingWhat it sets
Bed X × Y × ZThe printer's build volume: the bed check, Show Bed, Split for Printing
Nozzle diameter, extrusion width, layer heightThe smallest walls (2 extrusion widths), the bridging steps
Overhang limitHow steep a face may face down, from vertical, without support (45° on FDM printers)
Longest bridgeThe widest ceiling the printer can bridge
Hole clearanceAdded each side to nut pockets
Fits: press, snug, sliding, looseThe gaps Fit Clearance uses (0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5 mm to start)
Density, filament diameterThe mass and filament length in the check
Smallest hole, pin and gapThe small-feature checks
The material shrinksA warning about warping on long bases (ABS, ASA, nylon)

Four profiles come with RazorCAD: PLA, PETG and ABS on a 0.4 mm nozzle, and a resin printer. They can't be changed: Copy… one and change the copy. Use for this part keeps the choice with the part (a copy of the profile is saved in the part file too); Make default is the profile for parts that have none. A change to one of your profiles applies to every part that uses it.

Printer sets the bed from a list of popular printers (Prusa MK4 / MK4S, CORE One, CORE One L, XL and MINI+; Bambu Lab A1 mini, A1, P1S, X1C and H2D; Creality Ender-3 V3 and K1 Max; Elegoo Neptune 4 Pro; Anycubic Kobra 3). The Prusa sizes are from Prusa's own pages; the others are from retailers' and reviewers' listings, and the dialog says so when one is chosen: check them against your printer's specifications. Typing a bed size of your own clears the printer.

Slicer program (Windows app): Choose slicer program… picks the program Open in Slicer starts.

sections.title: Place on Bed, Auto-Orient and Show Bed
sections.text: The checks, the overhang map and the export all use the part's build orientation : which way up it prints. Until you set one, the part's biggest flat outside face lies on the bed. Place on Bed : select a flat face, then click it: that face goes down on the bed. Auto-Orient : tries the part with each of its outside flat faces down, and in the 26 directions of a cube's faces, edges and corners, and lists the best three: least support first, then the most on the bed, then the lowest. Use sets one. Show Bed : draws the printer's bed (a 10 mm grid) and its build volume under the part. Features that depend on which way is up (Printable Hole, Bridging Layer, First-Layer Chamfer, Printable Overhangs) keep the orientation the part had when they were added.

  • Auto-Orient : tries the part with each of its outside flat faces down, and in the 26 directions of a cube's faces, edges and corners, and lists the best three: least support first, then the most on the bed, then the lowest. Use sets one.

sections.title: Check Printability
sections.text: Check Printability checks the solid bodies in their build orientation against the profile, numbers what it finds on the model, and lists it: Check Fails when --- --- Overhangs A face facing down steeper than the overhang limit, off the bed (amber within 10° of it) Bridges A flat ceiling wider, the narrow way across, than the longest bridge Walls Thinner than 2 extrusion widths (amber under 3) Holes and pins A hole standing up under the smallest hole, a pin under the smallest pin Closed hollows A void sealed inside the part (a warning on FDM printers; a fail on resin, which is trapped in it) Bed contact Less than 5 % of the part's footprint on the bed Bed fit Bigger than the printer Warping A base over 150 mm long in a material that shrinks (a warning) Below the list: the support it would need (an estimate: columns from each overhang down to the part or the bed), the part's volume, its mass in the profile's material, and the filament it takes. Where a print feature fixes what was found, a button starts it: Printable Overhangs, Split for Printing, Auto-Orient.

sections.title: Overhang Map and Thickness Map
sections.text: Overhang Map colours the model up its build direction: green fine (or on the bed), amber within 10° of the profile's overhang limit, red over it (needs support). Thickness Map colours walls red under 2 extrusion widths, green to yellow above. Click again to turn them off.

sections.title: Nut Pocket
sections.text: Nut Pocket makes a hex pocket for an ISO 4032 nut, with the screw's clearance hole through (ISO 273 normal fit; untick it to leave it out). Click points on a face, or pick a sketch with points: each gets one. The pocket is the nut's size plus the profile's clearance each side, as deep as the nut plus the clearance (or Pocket depth). Turn the flats by turns it. Captive slot: the pocket starts Slot below the face inside the part and a slot as wide as the nut runs out sideways past the part's edge (Slot direction), to slide the nut in from the side.

sections.title: Insert Hole
sections.text: Insert Hole makes a hole for a threaded insert pressed or melted in (heat-set): the insert's hole diameter, as deep as the insert plus a Relief below it, with a lead-in Chamfer at the top. The sizes come from a table of typical inserts; makers' sizes differ, so check yours and type its Hole diameter and Insert length if they do.

sections.title: Screw Hole for Plastic
sections.text: Screw Hole for Plastic makes a pilot hole for a screw cut straight into the print: 0.85 × the screw's size (or a Pilot hole of your own), to a Depth, with a cap screw's Counterbore or a Countersink if wanted (ISO sizes).

sections.title: Printable Hole
sections.text: Printable Hole reshapes holes lying on their side so they print without support: their top comes to a 45° point up the build direction (a Teardrop), or the point is cut flat at the top of the hole. Every hole whose axis lies within Holes within this of level is changed, or click the holes to change only those.

Every hole whose axis lies within Holes within this of level is changed, or click the holes to change only those.

sections.title: Bridging Layer
sections.text: Bridging Layer helps a counterbore or pocket printed upside down: the printer can't bridge round the smaller hole above it. Click the flat face round the hole (the counterbore's floor). Steps: that face is stepped up one layer at a time, first a strip as wide as the hole across the opening, then a square, so each layer bridges onto the one before. A skin: one layer closes the hole; drill it out after printing.

sections.title: First-Layer Chamfer
sections.text: First-Layer Chamfer chamfers every edge on the bed (0.4 mm to start), so the first layer, squashed wider, doesn't stick out.
sections.html: First-Layer Chamfer chamfers every edge on the bed (0.4 mm to start), so the first layer, squashed wider, doesn't stick out.

sections.title: Printable Overhangs
sections.text: Printable Overhangs turns rounds facing down, up the build direction, into 45° chamfers of the same size, which print without support.
sections.html: Printable Overhangs turns rounds facing down, up the build direction, into 45° chamfers of the same size, which print without support.

sections.title: Fit Clearance
sections.text: Fit Clearance moves the faces of a part that fit against another part back by a fit's gap: Press, Snug, Sliding or Loose from the profile, or a Gap of your own. A flat face moves in; a pin gets thinner and a hole wider, by the gap all round.

sections.title: Print-in-Place Hinge
sections.text: Print-in-Place Hinge makes a hinge that prints assembled. Click the straight edge it turns about: knuckles (Knuckle diameter) are spaced along it, the gap apart; the first, third… carry the Pin all along, the others are bored the gap wider all round and turn on it. Each set is a body of its own: join each to its part with Combine.

sections.title: Split for Printing
sections.text: Split for Printing cuts a part too big for the printer in two at a plane (choose a plane, or click a flat face), with Dowels across the cut: holes for dowels (Dowel diameter, the profile's snug fit each side, Hole depth each side), spaced along the cut's longest side and kept clear of its edges. Glue the halves on the dowels.
sections.html: Split for Printing cuts a part too big for the printer in two at a plane (choose a plane, or click a flat face), with Dowels across the cut: holes for dowels (Dowel diameter, the profile's snug fit each side, Hole depth each side), spaced along the cut's longest side and kept clear of its edges. Glue the halves on the dowels.

sections.title: Export for Printing and Open in Slicer
sections.text: Export for Printing writes the solid bodies as 3MF (it keeps millimetres and each body as its own object), turned into their build orientation, their lowest point on the bed, over the bed's middle. Export STL for Printing does the same as STL. Open in Slicer (Windows app) opens the last export, or a new one, in the slicer program named in Print Profile; RazorCAD only starts the program with the file.

sections.title: Calibrate Fits
sections.text: Calibrate Fits saves a test piece (3MF): a plate with four Ø6 holes and four pegs, 6 mm less twice the profile's press, snug, sliding and loose gaps, left to right. Print it, try the pegs in the holes, and set each fit to the gap of the peg that fitted that way. Save the fits keeps them in the profile (a starting profile: in a copy of it, used by this part).

sections.title: Configurations
sections.text: A configuration is a variant of a part or assembly: other values for the global variables and other features suppressed in a part, other part configurations and components shown in an assembly.
sections.html: A configuration is a variant of a part or assembly: other values for the global variables and other features suppressed in a part, other part configurations and components shown in an assembly.

sections.title: The Configurations tab
sections.text: The Configurations tab sits next to the Feature tree and the Property panel at the top of the left panel. It lists Default and every configuration, the one shown ticked, each with a summary of what it changes. Double-click a configuration to show it. The tree shows its name next to the part. + Add Configuration makes a new one starting from the one shown. Right-click for Show Configuration, Rename, Copy Configuration, Properties (Design Table) and Delete.
sections.html:

  • Double-click a configuration to show it. The tree shows its name next to the part.
  • + Add Configuration makes a new one starting from the one shown.
  • Right-click for Show Configuration, Rename, Copy Configuration, Properties (Design Table) and Delete.

sections.title: What a part configuration changes
sections.text: Variable values: each configuration can give the global variables (Tools ▸ Equations) other values. Suppressed features: while a configuration is shown, Suppress / Unsuppress in the tree changes that configuration only. The tree greys out what it suppresses.
sections.html:
• Variable values: each configuration can give the global variables (Tools ▸ Equations) other values.
  • Suppressed features: while a configuration is shown, Suppress / Unsuppress in the tree changes that configuration only. The tree greys out what it suppresses.

sections.title: Design table
sections.text: Design Table… in the Configurations tab (or right-click ▸ Properties (Design Table), or Configurations on the Evaluate tab) edits all the configurations in one table. The table can be copied to and pasted from a spreadsheet as CSV.
sections.html: Design Table… in the Configurations tab (or right-click ▸ Properties (Design Table), or Configurations on the Evaluate tab) edits all the configurations in one table. The table can be copied to and pasted from a spreadsheet as CSV.

sections.title: Configurations in assemblies
sections.text: Assemblies have the same tab. While an assembly configuration is shown, these change that configuration only: a component's part configuration, Hide / Show, Suppress (a suppressed component is left out, with its mates) and a mate's Suppress or value. See the Assemblies chapter for how components use part configurations.

While an assembly configuration is shown, these change that configuration only: a component's part configuration, Hide / Show, Suppress (a suppressed component is left out, with its mates) and a mate's Suppress or value. See the Assemblies chapter for how components use part configurations.

sections.title: Assemblies
sections.text: An assembly places parts and other assemblies as components and holds them together with mates. Assemblies are saved as .rasm files and open in a tab of their own.
sections.html: An assembly places parts and other assemblies as components and holds them together with mates. Assemblies are saved as .rasm files and open in a tab of their own.

sections.title: Starting an assembly
sections.text: File ▸ New Assembly, or New Assembly in the start window. Every assembly has the standard Front, Top and Right Planes and the Origin at the top of its tree. They show in the view as a part's do (the eye in the tree, View ▸ Show Planes), and mates can use them; they stay where they are. The Assembly tab of the ribbon holds Insert Components, Standard Parts, Equations, Assembly Hole, Assembly Cut, Mate, Fix, Float, Hide Component, Suppress, Open Part, Edit in Context, Exploded View, Positions, Explode / Collapse, Motion Study, Bill of Materials, Interference Check, Collision Detection, Speed Mode and Zoom to Fit.
sections.html:

The Assembly tab of the ribbon holds Insert Components, Standard Parts, Equations, Assembly Hole, Assembly Cut, Mate, Fix, Float, Hide Component, Suppress, Open Part, Edit in Context, Exploded View, Positions, Explode / Collapse, Motion Study, Bill of Materials, Interference Check, Collision Detection, Speed Mode and Zoom to Fit.

sections.title: Inserting components
sections.text: Insert Components lists the parts and assemblies open in other tabs, or Browse for a Part or Assembly… takes a .rcad or .rasm file. The first component is fixed at the origin; the others are placed beside what is there. If the part has configurations, you choose which one to use. Right-click a component later to switch it to another configuration. The same part can be in the assembly several times in different configurations. The assembly keeps a copy of each part, refreshed from its tab or file whenever you come back to the assembly, so edit a part and the assembly follows. Several instances of one part share it: it is built once and drawn once.
sections.html:
Insert Components lists the parts and assemblies open in other tabs, or Browse for a Part or Assembly… takes a .rcad or .rasm file.

  • The first component is fixed at the origin; the others are placed beside what is there.
  • If the part has configurations, you choose which one to use. Right-click a component later to switch it to another configuration. The same part can be in the assembly several times in different configurations.
  • The assembly keeps a copy of each part, refreshed from its tab or file whenever you come back to the assembly, so edit a part and the assembly follows.
  • Several instances of one part share it: it is built once and drawn once.

sections.title: Standard parts
sections.text: Standard Parts (Assembly tab, or Insert ▸ Standard Parts…) adds parts made to size from their standards: hex bolts (ISO 4017) and socket head cap screws (ISO 4762), M3–M24, in the standard lengths; hex nuts (ISO 4032) and washers (ISO 7089); inch hex bolts (ASME B18.2.1), socket head cap screws (ASME B18.3), hex nuts (ASME B18.2.2) and SAE flat washers, 1/4" to 1", with UNC threads and inch lengths; socket set screws (ISO 4026), dowel pins (ISO 8734), round head rivets (ISO 1051), circlips for shafts and bores (DIN 471 / 472), parallel keys (DIN 6885 A) and 6000 / 6200 series ball bearings. Each is an ordinary part with its threads as cosmetic threads, so it builds fast. Choose its material: steel, stainless, brass or aluminium. The same type, size, length and material is one part however many times it is used, so the bill of materials counts them. Select a hole first (its round face or edge) and the size is picked to fit it (a clearance or tapped hole for bolts, the bore for a bearing, the shaft for a key), the length to suit the hole, and the part goes into the hole at the end facing you, mated to it (Concentric, plus Coincident on the face round the hole). For a bolt or screw: Washer under the head, and washer and nut on the far side: the whole set is mated, and the length is picked for it (a 10 mm plate: M8 × 25). All matching holes: the same part or set goes into every hole of the same size parallel to the selected one, in one go. A hole that ends on a curved face (a cross hole in a round bar) gets a seat plane of its own, which follows the hole when the part changes.

sections.title: Mates
sections.text: Click Mate (M), then two faces, edges or vertices on different components (or a standard plane), choose the type and click ✔. The panel stays open for the next mate; Esc closes it. Mate Holds --- --- Coincident Faces, edges or points together Concentric Axes in line Parallel / Perpendicular Directions Tangent A face touching a round face Distance / Angle At a set value Lock One component fixed to another Gear Two gears turning together: pick their cylinders (pitch circles) Rack Pinion A pinion turning as a rack slides: pick the pinion's cylinder and a straight edge or the flat face of the rack Screw On one axis, the second component advancing the pitch along it per turn it makes relative to the first (a nut on a lead screw) Width The second component centred between two faces of the first: pick a face of each, then the first component's other face, then the second's (two parallel faces each: a tongue in a slot) Slot A pin (a cylinder's axis) or a point kept the set distance from a straight edge (0: on it; the slot's side edge with the pin's radius), free to slide between the edge's ends and stopped there Path A point (a vertex, an edge's middle, a sphere's centre) kept on a curved or circular edge of another component, free to move along it Cam A follower kept touching a cam's curved edge (a plate cam's outline): a roller (a cylinder's axis) its radius from the edge, seen along the roller's axis, or a point at the set distance. Guide the follower with another mate (a Slot or a Concentric on a pivot) and turn the cam: the follower rides on it Symmetric Two faces, edges or vertices kept mirror images of each other about a plane: pick them, then the plane (or a flat face) between them Flat faces count as planes; cylinders, cones and circular edges as axes; spheres and vertices as points. Each mate is shown applied while you choose. Flip swaps Aligned / Anti-Aligned (or the side for Distance and Tangent). When the alignment chosen from how the faces sit can't be reached, the other one is used. Limit (Distance and Angle) : free between a Minimum and a Maximum instead of one value (a slide with end stops, a door that opens 0 to 110°). Inside the limits the component moves freely; dragged past one, it stays there exactly. A mate that conflicts with the others is refused with a message. A mate keeps its faces and edges by their geometry, not only by their number in the part. When a part gets a new feature or a dimension moves a face, the mate stays on the same face. A mate whose face or edge is gone gets a red ! in the tree ("1 mate lost a face"). Tools ▸ Fix Mates… lists them with Edit, Suppress and Delete.

sections.title: Gear and rack-pinion mates
sections.text: These relate one component's motion to another's, from where they are when the mate is made, so set the teeth in mesh first. Hold each gear on its axle with the usual mates (Concentric and Coincident); the gear mate then takes one more degree of freedom. Gear: turn one gear and the other turns the other way, in the ratio of their radii. Ratio is how many turns entity 2 makes per turn of entity 1; change it to the teeth ratio if the cylinders are not the pitch circles. Reverse the direction is for an internal gear, where both turn the same way. The tree shows it as for example "Gear1 1:2". Rack Pinion: turning the pinion slides the rack along the edge (or face) picked, and sliding the rack turns the pinion. Rack travel per pinion turn starts as the pinion's circumference (π × diameter). Reverse changes the direction. They follow turns of any size made step by step, as when you drag a gear. One jump of more than half a turn can't be told from a turn the other way.
sections.html:
These relate one component's motion to another's, from where they are when the mate is made, so set the teeth in mesh first. Hold each gear on its axle with the usual mates (Concentric and Coincident); the gear mate then takes one more degree of freedom.

  • Gear: turn one gear and the other turns the other way, in the ratio of their radii. Ratio is how many turns entity 2 makes per turn of entity 1; change it to the teeth ratio if the cylinders are not the pitch circles. Reverse the direction is for an internal gear, where both turn the same way. The tree shows it as for example "Gear1 1:2".
  • Rack Pinion: turning the pinion slides the rack along the edge (or face) picked, and sliding the rack turns the pinion. Rack travel per pinion turn starts as the pinion's circumference (π × diameter). Reverse changes the direction.
  • They follow turns of any size made step by step, as when you drag a gear. One jump of more than half a turn can't be told from a turn the other way.

sections.title: Moving components
sections.text: Left-drag a component to move it, Alt+drag to turn it. It moves only as its mates allow. The view turns, pans and zooms as in a part (see Navigating the 3D View). Selecting works as in a part and follows the selection filter: with no filter a click picks the vertex, edge, face or plane under the cursor; with the Bodies filter it picks whole components. Ctrl+click adds or takes away. Right-click a face, edge or vertex for Mate… and the component's commands; whatever is selected goes into the mate. Dragging a component moves it, whatever is selected.

Dragging a component moves it, whatever is selected.

sections.title: Fasten All Holes
sections.text: Fasten All Holes (Assembly tab) finds every stack of lined-up round holes through two or more components (tick Also holes through one component only for single ones too) and puts a fastener in each: the type you choose (hex bolt, socket head cap screw, inch sizes…), its size fitted to the holes, its length to the whole stack, with a washer under the head and a washer and nut on the far side if ticked, each mated in place (concentric, seated on the stack's outer faces). Stacks that have a fastener already are left alone, so it can be run again after adding parts.
sections.html: Fasten All Holes (Assembly tab) finds every stack of lined-up round holes through two or more components (tick Also holes through one component only for single ones too) and puts a fastener in each: the type you choose (hex bolt, socket head cap screw, inch sizes…), its size fitted to the holes, its length to the whole stack, with a washer under the head and a washer and nut on the far side if ticked, each mated in place (concentric, seated on the stack's outer faces). sections.title: Component patterns and mirrors
sections.text: Component Pattern, Circular Component Pattern and Mirror Components (Assembly tab) copy the selected component (or the components of the selected faces and edges) : Component Pattern: along X, Y, Z or a selected straight edge or axis, a spacing and a number of instances, and optionally a second direction. Circular Component Pattern: round X, Y, Z or a selected axis (a cylinder, a circular edge), a total angle (equal spacing) or the angle between copies. Mirror Components: about the YZ, XZ or XY plane or a selected flat face. The copy is placed as the mirror image, the part itself the same way round (for parts that are the same both ways round, such as screws, pins and brackets symmetric about the plane). The copies are components of their own (in the bill of materials, mateable), fixed, and follow their seed when it moves. The pattern is listed in the tree: double-click it to change it, or delete it with its copies.
sections.html:
Component Pattern, Circular Component Pattern and Mirror Components (Assembly tab) copy the selected component (or the components of the selected faces and edges) :

  • Component Pattern: along X, Y, Z or a selected straight edge or axis, a spacing and a number of instances, and optionally a second direction.
  • Circular Component Pattern: round X, Y, Z or a selected axis (a cylinder, a circular edge), a total angle (equal spacing) or the angle between copies.
  • Mirror Components: about the YZ, XZ or XY plane or a selected flat face. The copy is placed as the mirror image, the part itself the same way round (for parts that are the same both ways round, such as screws, pins and brackets symmetric about the plane).

The copies are components of their own (in the bill of materials, mateable), fixed, and follow their seed when it moves. The pattern is listed in the tree: double-click it to change it, or delete it with its copies.

sections.title: Collision detection
sections.text: Collision Detection on the Assembly tab (or Tools ▸ Collision Detection Off / Show Collisions While Dragging / Stop at Collisions While Dragging) checks for parts running into each other as you drag. Show: the parts that collide turn red while you drag, and the status bar names them. Stop: the dragged component (and what its mates carry along) stops where it meets the other part, right against it. Faces that only touch (mated faces) are not collisions, nor is a shaft in a hole of its size, nor a screw in a nut or tapped hole (threads are cosmetic, so the screw is its full diameter in a bore of about its minor diameter). Parts that already overlap when the drag starts are left out. It works from the parts' display meshes, so it keeps up with the mouse. Interference Check gives the exact overlap volumes.
sections.html:

sections.title: The assembly tree
sections.text: Each component shows (f) when fixed or (-) while still free to move, its configuration, and an eye to hide or show it. The Mates folder lists the mates; right-click one for Edit, Flip, Suppress or Delete. Right-click a component for Mate…, Open Part (or double-click it), Edit in Context…, Fix / Float, Hide / Show, Suppress / Unsuppress, Insert Another Instance, Rename and Delete. Make Flexible (a sub-assembly component) : its parts move in this assembly as its own mates let them (a hinge opening, a slide moving), solved with this assembly's mates on them; where they end up is kept with this component, so the sub-assembly itself and its other uses do not change. Make Rigid puts it back as one piece. A component fixed inside it stays fixed only when the sub-assembly component is fixed. Number Parts (Assembly tab) gives each part and sub-assembly a Part Number property in the order of the bill of materials: a prefix, a first number, a step and a number of digits (P-0001, P-0002…). Those with a part number keep it unless you ask to number them again. Save parts kept in files of their own to keep their numbers there. Edit in Context opens the part with the other parts you tick brought into it as transparent context bodies (the features Context: …), where they are in the assembly from it. Design the part to fit them: sketch on their faces, convert their edges, extrude up to them. Context bodies are references only: they are left out of the part where it is used (in the assembly, drawings, the bill of materials and exports). The context stays up to date: each time the part comes to the front with the assembly open, context bodies whose parts changed, changed configuration or moved are brought in again (a part taken out of the assembly has its context feature suppressed). Right-click a context feature ▸ Update Context to bring them all in again. Delete or suppress the context features when they are no longer needed. Save the part to update the assembly. Undo and redo work in the assembly.
