sections.title: Sub-assemblies
sections.text: An assembly can hold other assemblies as components. Insert Components ▸ Browse for a Part or Assembly… takes a .rasm file, and STEP assemblies keep their sub-assemblies when they open as an assembly. An assembly can't go inside itself. A sub-assembly is kept whole, with its own parts, placements and configurations, and moves, hides, suppresses and explodes as one. Clicking any of its parts picks it. Mates can use the faces, edges and vertices of the parts inside it. In the tree, ▶ opens a sub-assembly to show its components. Double-click one, or right-click the sub-assembly ▸ Open Sub-assembly, to change it in its own tab; the changes come back to the assembly.
sections.html:
An assembly can hold other assemblies as components. Insert Components ▸ Browse for a Part or Assembly… takes a .rasm file, and STEP assemblies keep their sub-assemblies when they open as an assembly. An assembly can't go inside itself.

  • A sub-assembly is kept whole, with its own parts, placements and configurations, and moves, hides, suppresses and explodes as one. Clicking any of its parts picks it.
  • Mates can use the faces, edges and vertices of the parts inside it.
  • In the tree, ▶ opens a sub-assembly to show its components. Double-click one, or right-click the sub-assembly ▸ Open Sub-assembly, to change it in its own tab; the changes come back to the assembly.

sections.title: Equations shared with the parts
sections.text: Assembly ▸ Equations… (also on the Assembly tab) holds the assembly's own variables, for example base = 6 and thickness = 2base. A variable that drives the parts sets the variable of the same name in every part that has one, through the sub-assemblies, so related parts are sized together from the top. The table shows each variable's value, the parts it drives and a Drives the parts check box (off for a variable used only to work out others). The values go into the assembly's copies of the parts, so the assembly, its drawings, the BOM and exports use them. They are applied again when a part is read again from its file. Update Open Parts writes them into the parts open in tabs too, to be saved there.
sections.html:
Assembly ▸ Equations… (also on the Assembly tab) holds the assembly's own variables, for example base = 6 and thickness = 2*base. A variable that drives the parts sets the variable of the same name in every part that has one, through the sub-assemblies, so related parts are sized together from the top.

  • The table shows each variable's value, the parts it drives and a Drives the parts check box (off for a variable used only to work out others).
  • The values go into the assembly's copies of the parts, so the assembly, its drawings, the BOM and exports use them. They are applied again when a part is read again from its file.
  • Update Open Parts writes them into the parts open in tabs too, to be saved there.

sections.title: Assembly holes and cuts
sections.text: Assembly Hole and Assembly Cut (Assembly tab, or the Insert menu) make holes and cuts in the assembly, through every component they pass. Click points on a flat face of a component. More points on the same face make more holes; clicking another face starts again. Set the hole: simple, counterbore, countersink or tapped, a standard size (ISO 273 close, normal or loose fit) or a custom one. The first component gets the hole as chosen, the ones behind it a plain hole of the drill size. Tap the last component makes the last one tapped for the size. A cut is a rectangle: width, length and angle. Choose Through all or a depth. Components cut lists the components it passes through; untick one to leave it out. Fasteners: hex bolts or socket head cap screws put into each hole as it is made, with washers and a nut on the far side if wanted, as long as the stack they hold (to a standard length) and mated in the hole. Into a tapped last component, a screw goes about one diameter into the thread, without a nut. The parts' own files are not changed: each component cut gets the feature in its copy of the part, so the assembly's drawings (hole callouts too), BOM and exports have the holes. The holes stay with the component they were clicked on: move a component and its holes are worked out again. The tree's Assembly Features folder lists them; right-click one to edit, suppress, rename or delete it. Fasteners put in a hole are kept when the hole is deleted.
sections.html:

The first component gets the hole as chosen, the ones behind it a plain hole of the drill size. Tap the last component makes the last one tapped for the size. A cut is a rectangle: width, length and angle.
  3. Choose Through all or a depth. Components cut lists the components it passes through; untick one to leave it out.
  4. Into a tapped last component, a screw goes about one diameter into the thread, without a nut.

The parts' own files are not changed: each component cut gets the feature in its copy of the part, so the assembly's drawings (hole callouts too), BOM and exports have the holes. The holes stay with the component they were clicked on: move a component and its holes are worked out again. The tree's Assembly Features folder lists them; right-click one to edit, suppress, rename or delete it. Fasteners put in a hole are kept when the hole is deleted.

sections.title: Exploded views
sections.text: Exploded View on the ribbon (or Insert ▸ Exploded View…) spreads components apart for display; the model and its mates stay put. Click components to pick them (click again to drop one). Pick a direction: ±X, ±Y, ±Z, or along a face's normal. Drag the picked items along the direction, or type the distance, then click Add Step. Spread Out spaces the picked items out along the direction, one step each. Click a step to change it, ✕ to delete it. Explode lines (dashed, from each item's place to where it is shown) can be switched off. The tree's Exploded Views folder lists them. Double-click one to explode or collapse it (animated); right-click for Explode / Collapse, Animate, Edit, Rename and Delete. The Explode / Collapse button on the ribbon does the same for the last one. Dragging a component, adding a mate or editing collapses the view first. Exploded views are saved with the file.
sections.html:
Exploded View on the ribbon (or Insert ▸ Exploded View…) spreads components apart for display; the model and its mates stay put.

  1. Click components to pick them (click again to drop one).
  2. Pick a direction: ±X, ±Y, ±Z, or along a face's normal.
  3. Drag the picked items along the direction, or type the distance, then click Add Step. Spread Out spaces the picked items out along the direction, one step each.
  4. Click a step to change it, ✕ to delete it. Explode lines (dashed, from each item's place to where it is shown) can be switched off.

The tree's Exploded Views folder lists them. Double-click one to explode or collapse it (animated); right-click for Explode / Collapse, Animate, Edit, Rename and Delete. The Explode / Collapse button on the ribbon does the same for the last one. Dragging a component, adding a mate or editing collapses the view first. Exploded views are saved with the file.

sections.title: Motion studies
sections.text: Motion Study (Assembly tab) shows how an assembly moves. Choose a driver: turning a component about the axis of one of its mates (360°, for example); sliding a component along one of its mates' axes or faces; changing a Distance or Angle mate's value from where it is to a new one. The motion is worked out step by step and the mates carry the other components along, gear and rack-pinion mates included. Play / Stop (Space), back to the start, a slider to go through the steps, the number of steps, the duration and Loop. Where the mates can't follow, the panel says at which step. Detect collisions (on for new studies) checks every step: parts that collide show in red as the motion plays, and the panel names the first collision and its step. Stop at the first collision ends the motion at the step before it. Clearance between two components (choose them in the panel) works out, at every step, the least distance between them from their display meshes, and the panel gives the least of all and its step (in red when they touch). ✔ keeps the study in the assembly's Motion Studies folder: double-click one to play it; right-click to edit, rename or delete it. Closing the panel puts the assembly back as it was: a motion study never moves the assembly itself.
sections.html:
Motion Study (Assembly tab) shows how an assembly moves. Choose a driver:

  • turning a component about the axis of one of its mates (360°, for example);
  • sliding a component along one of its mates' axes or faces;
  • changing a Distance or Angle mate's value from where it is to a new one.

The motion is worked out step by step and the mates carry the other components along, gear and rack-pinion mates included. Play / Stop (Space), back to the start, a slider to go through the steps, the number of steps, the duration and Loop. Where the mates can't follow, the panel says at which step.

Detect collisions (on for new studies) checks every step: parts that collide show in red as the motion plays, and the panel names the first collision and its step. Stop at the first collision ends the motion at the step before it. Clearance between two components (choose them in the panel) works out, at every step, the least distance between them from their display meshes, and the panel gives the least of all and its step (in red when they touch).

✔ keeps the study in the assembly's Motion Studies folder: double-click one to play it; right-click to edit, rename or delete it. Closing the panel puts the assembly back as it was: a motion study never moves the assembly itself.

sections.title: Interference Check
sections.text: Interference Check (Assembly tab, or Tools ▸ Interference Check…) finds where components overlap. Each overlap shows in red and is listed with its two components (inside sub-assemblies as "Sub-assembly ▸ Part") and its volume. Faces that only touch, such as mated faces, are not counted, and nor are the bodies of one multi-body part against each other. An exploded assembly is collapsed first, so the check is of where the mates put the parts.
sections.html: Interference Check (Assembly tab, or Tools ▸ Interference Check…) finds where components overlap. Each overlap shows in red and is listed with its two components (inside sub-assemblies as "Sub-assembly ▸ Part") and its volume. Faces that only touch, such as mated faces, are not counted, and nor are the bodies of one multi-body part against each other. An exploded assembly is collapsed first, so the check is of where the mates put the parts.

sections.title: Bill of Materials
sections.text: Bill of Materials lists the parts with their quantities and materials: one row per part and configuration used, with suppressed components left out. It is indented: a sub-assembly's parts are listed under it (1.1, 1.2…), with the quantities in one of it. Copy as CSV or Save CSV… takes it to a spreadsheet. Columns: click a column heading to change what it shows (an item number, quantity, part, material, file, configuration, any custom property, mass, cost, or values typed in), insert a column left or right, move, rename or remove it. Typed values are edited right in the table. The columns are kept with the assembly and are part of undo; Default Columns goes back to the usual ones. Mass and cost: Mass and Total mass come from each part's material and volume; Cost and Total cost from a part's Cost property (for example 12.50, $3 or R12,50). A TOTAL row adds up the quantity, mass and cost; a sub-assembly adds up its parts.
sections.html:
Bill of Materials lists the parts with their quantities and materials: one row per part and configuration used, with suppressed components left out. It is indented: a sub-assembly's parts are listed under it (1.1, 1.2…), with the quantities in one of it. Copy as CSV or Save CSV… takes it to a spreadsheet.

  • Columns: click a column heading to change what it shows (an item number, quantity, part, material, file, configuration, any custom property, mass, cost, or values typed in), insert a column left or right, move, rename or remove it. Typed values are edited right in the table. The columns are kept with the assembly and are part of undo; Default Columns goes back to the usual ones.
  • Mass and cost: Mass and Total mass come from each part's material and volume; Cost and Total cost from a part's Cost property (for example 12.50, $3 or R12,50). A TOTAL row adds up the quantity, mass and cost; a sub-assembly adds up its parts.

sections.title: STEP assemblies
sections.text: Opening a STEP file that holds an assembly asks whether to open it as an assembly or as one part (see Importing in the Working with Files chapter). As an assembly, each part of the file becomes a part, each sub-assembly a sub-assembly, and each component is placed, fixed, where the file places it, with the names and colours from the file. File ▸ Export ▸ STEP… in an assembly saves the whole assembly as one STEP file with its structure: each part once, in the configuration used, every component placed where it is and named after it, sub-assemblies kept as assemblies, and the parts' colours. Suppressed components are left out.
sections.html:
Opening a STEP file that holds an assembly asks whether to open it as an assembly or as one part (see Importing in the Working with Files chapter). As an assembly, each part of the file becomes a part, each sub-assembly a sub-assembly, and each component is placed, fixed, where the file places it, with the names and colours from the file.

File ▸ Export ▸ STEP… in an assembly saves the whole assembly as one STEP file with its structure: each part once, in the configuration used, every component placed where it is and named after it, sub-assemblies kept as assemblies, and the parts' colours. Suppressed components are left out.

sections.title: Saving parts as separate files
sections.text: When an assembly holds parts or sub-assemblies that are only inside it (as a STEP assembly does when it opens), Save asks how to save them: Save Parts as Separate Files saves each part as a .rcad file and each sub-assembly as a .rasm file in the assembly's folder, named after them. The assembly (and each sub-assembly) then uses those files, so each part can be opened and changed on its own and the change shows in the assembly. A part used in several places is one file. If files of those names are already there, you are asked before they are replaced. Save as One File keeps everything inside the assembly file. You are not asked again, except on Save As.
sections.html:
When an assembly holds parts or sub-assemblies that are only inside it (as a STEP assembly does when it opens), Save asks how to save them:

  • Save Parts as Separate Files saves each part as a .rcad file and each sub-assembly as a .rasm file in the assembly's folder, named after them. The assembly (and each sub-assembly) then uses those files, so each part can be opened and changed on its own and the change shows in the assembly. A part used in several places is one file. If files of those names are already there, you are asked before they are replaced.
  • Save as One File keeps everything inside the assembly file. You are not asked again, except on Save As.

sections.title: Collect Files
sections.text: File ▸ Collect Files… (in an assembly) copies the assembly with everything in it into one folder: each part and sub-assembly a file of its own (as the assembly has it now), the assembly last, using those files. Names can be given something before and after them (e.g. P1-), to start a variant of the design or send it all to someone. The assembly open here is left as it is.
sections.html: File ▸ Collect Files… (in an assembly) copies the assembly with everything in it into one folder: each part and sub-assembly a file of its own (as the assembly has it now), the assembly last, using those files. Names can be given something before and after them (e.g. P1-), to start a variant of the design or send it all to someone. The assembly open here is left as it is.

sections.title: Big assemblies
sections.text: Each part an assembly builds is kept in the model cache (%LOCALAPPDATA%\RazorCAD\modelcache). Opening the assembly again shows unchanged parts straight from there, and the kernel only builds parts that changed, so a large layout reopens in seconds. Parts are built side by side in several geometry kernels at once, as many as the PC's processor threads and memory allow, and each shows as soon as it is built. Each part is sent to the graphics card once and placed at every component that uses it, so moving, hiding or exploding components is instant. Speed Mode (Assembly tab, or View ▸ Speed Mode) is for very large assemblies: the parts are shown from simplified display meshes, with far fewer triangles to draw and keep in memory. The faces and edges stay the same, so mates, measuring, picking and collision detection work as before. A component you select is loaded in full; turning speed mode off shows everything in full again. It is saved with the assembly, and a large assembly suggests it in the status bar. Drawings, exports and Interference Check always use the exact geometry.

sections.title: Drawings
sections.text: RazorCAD makes 2D engineering drawings of parts and assemblies, saved as .rdrw files and opened in their own tab.
sections.html: RazorCAD makes 2D engineering drawings of parts and assemblies, saved as .rdrw files and opened in their own tab.

sections.title: Starting a drawing
sections.text: Start window ▸ New Drawing, or File ▸ New Drawing, opens the set-up dialog (below) and then an empty sheet. File ▸ Make Drawing from Part (in a part), or Make Drawing from Assembly (in an assembly): after the set-up dialog, places the standard three views at a scale that fits, clear of the title block. A drawing can show assemblies as well as parts: every component is drawn where it sits, through its sub-assemblies, in the configurations shown; suppressed and hidden components are left out. Big assemblies (more than about 200 solids) are drawn fast from the parts' display meshes: lines, circles and arcs as exact as the 3D view's, and where an edge turns hidden to about two thousandths of the view's size. A site layout of thousands of solids then takes seconds a view instead of many minutes. In a view's properties, Hidden lines chooses Automatic, Exact or Fast; section and flat-pattern views are always exact. Drawings are opened, saved and listed in the recent files like parts.

• Start window ▸ New Drawing, or File ▸ New Drawing, opens the set-up dialog (below) and then an empty sheet.
  • File ▸ Make Drawing from Part (in a part), or Make Drawing from Assembly (in an assembly): after the set-up dialog, places the standard three views at a scale that fits, clear of the title block.

Big assemblies (more than about 200 solids) are drawn fast from the parts' display meshes: lines, circles and arcs as exact as the 3D view's, and where an edge turns hidden to about two thousandths of the view's size. A site layout of thousands of solids then takes seconds a view instead of many minutes. In a view's properties, Hidden lines chooses Automatic, Exact or Fast; section and flat-pattern views are always exact.

Drawings are opened, saved and listed in the recent files like parts.

sections.title: The sheet and its template
sections.text: The default template is A3 with an ISO 5457 frame (zones and centring marks) and an ISO 7200-style title block: title, drawing number, material, scale, size, units, projection symbol, drawn / checked / approved, date, mass, company, revision, sheet n of m and general tolerances. Sheet sizes A0 to A4, landscape or portrait.
sections.html: The default template is A3 with an ISO 5457 frame (zones and centring marks) and an ISO 7200-style title block: title, drawing number, material, scale, size, units, projection symbol, drawn / checked / approved, date, mass, company, revision, sheet n of m and general tolerances. Sheet sizes A0 to A4, landscape or portrait.

sections.title: Drawing templates
sections.text: A drawing template (.rdrt file) keeps a drawing's set-up: its sheets (size, orientation, scale, projection), the drawing settings (text height, decimals…), the title block's standing entries (company, drawn / checked / approved by, finish, tolerances, revision) and notes placed on the sheet. Views, parts and part-specific entries (title, drawing number, material, mass, date) are not kept. File ▸ Save as Template… in a drawing saves one, by default to Documents\RazorCAD\Templates. Opening a .rdrt file edits the template in its own tab. The New Drawing dialog lists your templates (from the Templates folder, or Browse… for one anywhere) and the standard ones: A4 portrait and landscape, A3, A2, A1 and A0 landscape, and A3 and A4 in third angle projection. Set the drawing name, title, drawing number, drawn by and company, and the first sheet's size, orientation, scale and projection. Tick Use this template as my default to have it chosen first next time. Double-click a template to create the drawing at once. Change Template… (File menu, Sheet tab, or right-click the drawing in the tree) switches an existing drawing to another template. Views, dimensions and annotations stay; company, tolerance and finish come from the new template, and the old template's notes are replaced. Undo goes back. Company sheet formats: a template can carry its own border, title block and logo in place of the standard ISO one, used on sheets of its size and orientation. Its text shows the drawing's properties, and can be set in a font installed on the PC; PDF exports embed the font. Drawing Properties lists the title block's own fields. Changing the projection (Change Template or Sheet Properties) lays the views out again for the new projection, so a top view stays a top view.

sections.title: View Layout tab
sections.text: Command What it does --- --- Model View Pick an open part or assembly, or browse for its file (.rcad or .rasm), pick the orientation (front, back, top, bottom, left, right, isometric, dimetric, trimetric or flat pattern) and click on the sheet. Then move around it to place projected views. Standard Views Three views laid out for first- or third-angle projection Projected View A view aligned with its parent Flat Pattern A sheet metal body unfolded (see below) Section View Horizontal, vertical or At an angle (degrees from horizontal, counter-clockwise) cutting line, hatched cut faces, A-A labels and arrows, flip; an angled section looks square to its line and can be placed anywhere Detail View A circle with a letter, 2:1 by default Auxiliary View Looks square at an inclined edge, so it shows its true shape Break Leaves out the middle of a long part; dimensions across the break keep the true length Crop View Shows only the area you draw round Broken-out Section Click a view, then the corners of an outline round what to show inside; click the first corner again to close it and give the depth from the front of the model. The material inside the outline is taken away to that depth, the faces cut there hatched, the outline drawn thin. Right-click the view ▸ Remove Broken-out Section takes it away Compare With This drawing's sheets against another drawing open in RazorCAD (an earlier version, say), sheet by sheet: lines only in this one in red, only in the other in green, in both in grey Update Views Re-reads the parts and redraws the views A broken or cropped view can be put back to whole from its right-click menu. Section views hatch each body or component with its own angle and spacing. Views are hidden-line projections computed by the geometry kernel.

sections.title: View properties
sections.text: Click a view to open its panel: Orientation, changeable after placing (also to and from Flat Pattern; projected and section views made from it are removed when it becomes a flat pattern, and Ctrl+Z brings them back). Display style: hidden lines removed, hidden lines visible, or wireframe; tangent edges and cosmetic threads on or off. Exploded (a view of an assembly that has exploded views): shows the view exploded as one of them. The components are where that exploded view moves them, the view keeps its place on the sheet, and its projected, section, auxiliary and detail views follow. Balloons on it pick the moved parts. Alternate position (a view of an assembly): draws the assembly again as a position kept in it, in thin phantom lines (long dash, two short), over the view: a lid open, a lever at its other end. Keep positions in the assembly with Assembly ▸ Positions (move the components, e.g. by changing a mate, keep the position, then put them back). Sheet scale or a custom scale; labels. Rotate View: −90°, +90°, 180° and 0° buttons and an angle box (degrees, counter-clockwise). Section lines, detail circles and annotations turn with the view. Aligned views slide only along their alignment. Deleting a view deletes the views made from it.

sections.title: Flat pattern views
sections.text: A flat pattern view shows a sheet metal body unfolded with its outline and holes, bend lines (chain lines) with notes (UP / DOWN, angle, radius), optional bend region lines, and its flat size, thickness, number of bends and cut length underneath. It can be dimensioned (bend lines too) and exported to PDF. If the part has several sheet metal bodies, pick the body in the view properties. Instead of notes, the view can show a bend table: the bend lines numbered B1, B2… and a table of direction, angle and inside radius under the view. Forms, cross breaks and tabs and slots show as in the DXF.

sections.title: Annotation tab
sections.text: Command How --- --- Dimension Click a line for its length, a circle for its diameter (an arc: radius), two points, lines or circles for the distance between them (two lines at an angle: the angle), then click where the text goes. Horizontal, vertical or aligned depends on where you place it. Prefix, suffix, tolerance and override text can be set. Auto Dimension Dimensions the selected views, or every view on the sheet (see below) Check Drawing Lists what the drawing still lacks (see below) Note Click on the sheet; click an edge first to add a leader Baseline Dimension Click the base edge or point, then each point or edge to dimension from it; the dimensions stack one above the other Ordinate Dimension Click the origin, then where the values line up, then the points to dimension Chamfer Dimension Click the chamfer edge and an edge next to it, then place the text ("3 × 45°") Hole Callout Click a hole. The callout gives its size and depth from the Hole feature (counterbore, countersink, tapped thread and tap drill) or its cosmetic thread, and how many of the same holes the view shows, for example "4× Ø6.6 THRU ALL / CBORE Ø11 DEEP 6.5". Datum Feature A datum letter in a box, with a triangle on the feature Geometric Tolerance A feature control frame: one of the 14 characteristic symbols, tolerance with Ø zone and material condition, and up to three datums Surface Finish A surface finish symbol with its roughness Weld Symbol Fillet, square, V, bevel or plug weld on a reference line with an arrow to the joint; arrow, other or both sides; all-around, field weld and tail Center Mark Click circles or arcs Centerline Click two lines (or two points); the centerline runs between them Revision Table Rows edited in one dialog; the latest revision goes into the title block Table A general table : a title, rows (one a line, cells split by , or pasted from a spreadsheet with tabs), the first row a bold header if ticked; each column as wide as its widest cell. {material}, {title} and the drawing's other properties fill in. Double-click it to change it or delete it Cut List Table The cut list of the part in the selected view (see the Fast Structure chapter); it updates when the part changes Hole Table The holes of the selected view (circles seen end on) tagged in it, a letter for each size, largest first, numbered from the bottom left (A1, A2… B1), with their X and Y from the view's lower-left corner and their size; it updates when the part changes Balloon Click a part in a view, then where the balloon goes. The number is that part's item in the bill of materials, found from the part under the click (in a sub-assembly, the sub-assembly's item). Keep clicking for more; Esc ends. Where the part can't be told, it asks for the number. Right-click a balloon ▸ Item Number… to change it. BOM Table The bill of materials of the drawing's assembly: ITEM, QTY, PART and MATERIAL, at the top right of the sheet. Drag it anywhere; right-click it to show the sub-assemblies' parts (indented). It follows the assembly. Right-click a column to change what it shows (any field, custom property, mass, cost or typed values), insert, move, rename or remove it; double-click a typed value to edit it. Columns… (right-click the table, or double-click it) has everything in one dialog. With mass or cost columns a TOTAL row is added. Datum features, geometric tolerances, surface finish and weld symbols can each have a leader. Right-click one ▸ Edit… to change it.

sections.title: Auto Dimension
sections.text: Annotation ▸ Auto Dimension (also Insert ▸ Annotations) adds the dimensions the selected views need, or every view on the sheet's: the overall sizes, outermost; hole diameters, one per size ("4× Ø9"); arc radii; and hole positions. Each size is given once in the drawing, and nothing is added that a view's own dimensions already give. Only views looking along the part's axes are dimensioned. It asks how, and keeps your choices for next time: Positions: baseline (each from the view's edge), chain (edge to hole to hole on one row) or ordinate (values from the view's bottom left corner). Tolerance, for example ±0.1, added to the new lengths and diameters. Spread labels that would overlap. Add: which kinds (overall sizes, hole diameters, hole positions, arc radii). Everything it adds is one undo step; drag the dimensions to tidy them up.
sections.html:
Annotation ▸ Auto Dimension (also Insert ▸ Annotations) adds the dimensions the selected views need, or every view on the sheet's: the overall sizes, outermost; hole diameters, one per size ("4× Ø9"); arc radii; and hole positions. Each size is given once in the drawing, and nothing is added that a view's own dimensions already give. Only views looking along the part's axes are dimensioned.

It asks how, and keeps your choices for next time:

  • Positions: baseline (each from the view's edge), chain (edge to hole to hole on one row) or ordinate (values from the view's bottom left corner).
  • Tolerance, for example ±0.1, added to the new lengths and diameters.
  • Spread labels that would overlap.
  • Add: which kinds (overall sizes, hole diameters, hole positions, arc radii).

Everything it adds is one undo step; drag the dimensions to tidy them up.

sections.title: Check Drawing
sections.text: Annotation ▸ Check Drawing (or Tools ▸ Check Drawing…) lists what the drawing still lacks before it goes out, most important first: Title block: fields left empty. Title, drawing number, drawn by, date, revision and material are to fix; checked and approved are noted, to be filled in at sign-off. Dimensions per view: part views with no dimensions (a view whose sizes all show in other views is only noted), crowded views, annotations whose view was deleted and dimensions that lost what they measured. Undimensioned features: overall sizes, hole diameters, radii and hole positions that no dimension gives. A size given in one view is not asked for again in the part's other views, a hole callout gives a hole's diameter, and hole positions count in baseline, chain or ordinate style. Click an item to show its view or annotation. Add Missing Dimensions puts in what Auto Dimension would; Title Block… opens the drawing's properties.
sections.html:
Annotation ▸ Check Drawing (or Tools ▸ Check Drawing…) lists what the drawing still lacks before it goes out, most important first:

  • Title block: fields left empty. Title, drawing number, drawn by, date, revision and material are to fix; checked and approved are noted, to be filled in at sign-off.
  • Dimensions per view: part views with no dimensions (a view whose sizes all show in other views is only noted), crowded views, annotations whose view was deleted and dimensions that lost what they measured.
  • Undimensioned features: overall sizes, hole diameters, radii and hole positions that no dimension gives. A size given in one view is not asked for again in the part's other views, a hole callout gives a hole's diameter, and hole positions count in baseline, chain or ordinate style.

Click an item to show its view or annotation. Add Missing Dimensions puts in what Auto Dimension would; Title Block… opens the drawing's properties.

sections.title: DXF drawings on the sheet
sections.text: Insert ▸ DXF Drawing… places a DXF file's lines, circles, arcs, polylines, ellipses, splines and texts on the sheet as one item, in the middle of the frame at full size or scaled down to a standard scale that fits. Drag it, right-click ▸ Scale…, or delete it; it prints and exports with the sheet.

Drag it, right-click ▸ Scale…, or delete it; it prints and exports with the sheet.

sections.title: Sheet tab
sections.text: Sheet Properties: size, orientation, scale, first or third angle. Title Block (Drawing Properties): title block fields, text height and decimals. Units: click MMGS / IPS in the status bar. An inch drawing gives lengths in inches with three decimals and its title block says "in"; angles are not converted. Change Template: see Drawing templates above. Add Sheet: drawings can have several sheets, shown as tabs under the sheet. Export PDF: vector PDF, one page per sheet. Export DXF: the current sheet as a DXF file, with layers for visible, thin, hidden and centre lines, text and hatching. A sheet format's logo is left out.
sections.html:
• Sheet Properties: size, orientation, scale, first or third angle.
  • Title Block (Drawing Properties): title block fields, text height and decimals.
  • Units: click MMGS / IPS in the status bar. An inch drawing gives lengths in inches with three decimals and its title block says "in"; angles are not converted.
  • Change Template: see Drawing templates above.
  • Add Sheet: drawings can have several sheets, shown as tabs under the sheet.
  • Export PDF: vector PDF, one page per sheet.
  • Export DXF: the current sheet as a DXF file, with layers for visible, thin, hidden and centre lines, text and hatching. A sheet format's logo is left out.

sections.title: Views follow the part
sections.text: Views and dimensions follow changes to the part or assembly, whether it is open in another tab or read from its file. A copy of the part is kept in the drawing so it still opens if the part file is missing.

sections.title: Measure
sections.text: Evaluate ▸ Measure, Tools ▸ Measure… or the view's right-click menu. Click vertices, edges, faces, planes or sketch lines; with two items picked it shows the distance between them plus dX, dY and dZ. Use the body filter (B) to pick whole bodies. Sizes are in the document's units. Snap To: besides vertices, a click picks sketch points, the midpoints of edges and the centres of circles and arcs (a hole's centre too); each can be turned off. As you move, the point a click would pick is marked on the model with its name. The items picked are numbered 1 and 2 on the model. Keep the first item measures from the first item to each next click (a third click replaces the second, not the first). Measured lists the distances measured so far, most recent first.

sections.title: DFM Check
sections.text: Evaluate ▸ DFM Check checks the solids for machining : sharp inside corners (a concave straight edge between flat faces: a cutter leaves its radius there), inside rounds smaller than the smallest cutter radius, holes smaller than the smallest hole or deeper than a number of times their diameter, hole sizes that are not standard drills (whole or half millimetres up to 20, whole millimetres above: reamed, bored or clearance holes are reported as notes), and very small faces (often import slivers). Each finding is listed and numbered on the model; Clear the marks removes them. For thin walls use Thickness Analysis, for moulded parts Draft Analysis and Undercut Check, for sheet metal Sheet Metal Check.

sections.title: 3D Annotations
sections.text: Evaluate ▸ 3D Annotation puts product and manufacturing information on the model itself (model based definition) : a Note, a Dimension between two points (its value measured, or given) with its tolerances, a Geometric tolerance (a feature control frame: the characteristic, a Ø zone if ticked, the tolerance and the datums), a Datum letter or a Surface finish (Ra). Fill in the dialog, then click the point on the model it is about (two points for a dimension). Each shows as a label with a leader to its point and follows the view. Tools ▸ 3D Annotations… lists them, to delete them or hide them all. Exported to STEP (whole part), datums, geometric tolerances and dimensions go into the file as semantic PMI (AP242), each on the face it points at, for programs that read AP242 PMI; notes and surface finishes go in as properties of the part. A STEP file with PMI opened in RazorCAD shows its datums, tolerances and dimensions as 3D annotations. They are saved with the part, and a STEP export of the part carries them: each annotation is written as a property of the part with its kind, its text and the points it refers to (the file is AP242). Programs that read STEP properties show them; they are not semantic GD&T that a measuring machine program can use directly.

sections.title: Tolerance Stack-Up
sections.text: Evaluate ▸ Tolerance Stack-Up (also in an assembly's ribbon, and Tools ▸ Tolerance Stack-Up…) works out a gap from a chain of dimensions in one direction . Each row is a dimension: its nominal size, its upper and lower tolerance (both as positive numbers: 50 +0.1 / −0) and whether it adds to or takes from the gap. The results update as you type: the gap's nominal and mean, its worst case limits (every tolerance at its limit together) and its statistical limits (root sum of squares: what most assemblies see when the parts vary independently), checked against the gap required (at least / at most). The share column shows which tolerances matter most. Stack-ups are kept in the part or assembly; New stack-up adds another.

sections.title: Mass Properties
sections.text: Evaluate ▸ Mass Properties shows mass, volume, surface area and centre of mass. It adds up every body with its own density and lists the bodies. A body with no material uses 1.00 g/cm³.
sections.html: Evaluate ▸ Mass Properties shows mass, volume, surface area and centre of mass. It adds up every body with its own density and lists the bodies. A body with no material uses 1.00 g/cm³.

sections.title: Interference Check
sections.text: Evaluate ▸ Interference Check finds where the solid bodies of a part overlap. It lists each pair with its overlap volume and shows the overlaps in red. Assemblies have their own (see the Assemblies chapter).
sections.html: Evaluate ▸ Interference Check finds where the solid bodies of a part overlap. It lists each pair with its overlap volume and shows the overlaps in red. Assemblies have their own (see the Assemblies chapter).

sections.title: Surface analysis
sections.text: These displays colour the model to show the quality of its faces. Click the button again to turn its display off. Command Shows --- --- Zebra Stripes Reflected stripes on every body. Across a smooth join the stripes run on without a kink. Curvature Bodies coloured from blue (flat) through green and yellow to red (tightest). The status bar gives the radius red stands for. Draft Analysis Choose a pull direction (an axis or a selected face's normal) and the draft needed. Faces turn green with enough draft, yellow where they need more, and red with draft the other way. Thickness Analysis Give the thinnest and thickest walls allowed. Each point is coloured by the wall thickness measured from it straight in through the material: red thinner than allowed, blue thicker (sinks and voids in a moulding), green to yellow between, grey where no wall was found. The status bar gives the thinnest and thickest walls and the share of the surface outside the limits. Undercut Check Choose a pull direction. Each point is looked at along it and against it: green can be pulled out along it (one mould half), blue against it (the other), red neither way (an undercut, needing a side action or a change). The status bar gives the share of the surface undercut.

sections.title: Equations and global variables
sections.text: Tools ▸ Equations… holds global variables that can be used in any dimension or feature value. Example: width = 120, then set a depth to width/4. Each row shows the value it evaluates to; invalid or duplicate names are flagged. Every value field accepts: Item Examples --- --- Operators + - / ^ % and parentheses Variables Any name from Equations Trigonometry (degrees) sin cos tan asin acos atan Other functions sqrt abs min max round floor ceil pow Constants pi Units of length 2in, 30 mm, 1.5cm, 2ft, (w/2)in (see Units) A value may start with =. Variable names start with a letter or underscore and can't be a function name.

sections.title: Macros
sections.text: Tools ▸ Macros… writes, runs and saves JavaScript macros that drive RazorCAD. In parts they can sketch (lines, rectangles, circles, arcs, polygons), extrude, cut, revolve, add any feature, change or delete features, set equations and the material, and rebuild. In assemblies and drawings they can add, change and remove components, mates, views and annotations. Anywhere they can run any command by its name in the command search, ask you for a value, and run other macros. The API button lists what a macro can use; a sample macro shows the idea. A macro's changes are one undo step. Errors show their line, which is selected in the editor. Ctrl+Enter runs; Ctrl+S saves. Tools ▸ Record Macro records what you do until Stop Recording Macro (or the red "● Recording macro" in the status bar): the features you add, change, delete or reorder, the commands you run, and in assemblies and drawings what you change there (parts inserted, components moved, mates, views, annotations, sheets). The recording opens in the Macros dialog to be saved or edited. Items made during the recording are kept in variables and others are found by name, so a recording plays back into another part, assembly or drawing. Saved macros are in the Tools menu (Macro: name) and the command search, so they can have keyboard shortcuts. Import… / Export… share them as .js files. Warning: Macros can do anything RazorCAD can. Run only macros you trust.

sections.title: Setting up
sections.text: Open Tools ▸ Claude Settings… (or the Claude tab ▸ Claude Settings) and choose how RazorCAD reaches Claude: My Claude subscription (Claude Code on this PC): each request goes through the Claude Code command-line program installed on this PC, signed in to your own Claude Pro or Max plan. It counts toward that plan's usage limits, with no separate bill. The dialog shows where Claude Code was found, its version and whether it is signed in; Sign In… starts the sign-in, which you finish in the browser, and Check Again reads the status again. Claude Code runs with no tools, settings or memory, from an empty folder, so it sees only RazorCAD's modelling guide and your request. An Anthropic API key: enter your own key (create one at console.anthropic.com ▸ API Keys; requests are billed to that account). The key is stored on this PC in %APPDATA%\RazorCAD\claude.json and is only sent to api.anthropic.com. Remove Key deletes it. Then choose a model: Opus, Sonnet or Haiku.

sections.title: Ask Claude panel
sections.text: Open it with the Claude tab ▸ Ask Claude, or Tools ▸ Ask Claude…. Describe a part or a change. Claude adds the features to the tree; each answer is one undo step. If the features don't build, Claude is told the error and corrects it, up to two more tries. Claude sees the feature list and body sizes of the part, not the picture. New Conversation (or New chat in the panel) starts fresh; the part stays as it is. The model can be switched in the panel.

sections.title: Crash reports
sections.text: RazorCAD writes a crash report whenever something goes wrong, to %APPDATA%\RazorCAD\crashes\ _ \. Open the folder with Help ▸ Open Crash Reports Folder. The start window mentions new reports. The newest 30 are kept. File Contents --- --- report.json The kind of failure, the error message and stack trace, what RazorCAD was doing (mode, Property panel, sketch tool, selection, feature errors) and system information session.log The recent actions of the session, newest last part.rcad The part that was open, so the problem can be reproduced Kinds of report: ui-error, kernel-error, kernel-worker-crash, python-exception, native-crash and unexpected-shutdown (a session that ended without closing normally, found at the next launch).

sections.title: Reporting a problem
sections.text: Help ▸ Report a Problem…, or Report on GitHub… in the start window's crash notice, turns a crash report (or a plain description, without a crash) into a GitHub issue. The report holds RazorCAD's version, Windows, what went wrong and the last lines of the session log; you see the whole text first and can edit it. Your user name and folders are taken out, and the part you were working on is not included. Open GitHub Issue opens RazorCAD's new-issue page in your browser with the text filled in; nothing is sent until you submit it there. Copy Text copies it instead.

sections.title: Speed on your PC
sections.text: How many geometry kernels work at once comes from the PC RazorCAD runs on: one per processor thread beyond two (left for the window and the rest of the PC), and about 1 GB of free memory each beyond 2 GB, read from Windows when RazorCAD starts; at least 2, at most 16. Assemblies build their parts side by side in them, drawings draw their views in them, and each open part keeps one (up to half of them). Kernels that are idle for a few minutes are stopped to give their memory back. A big imported STEP file's bodies are meshed by several kernels at once when that is quicker (64 bodies with 6784 faces: 1.8 s instead of 5.4 s). Crash reports note the figures, for example "up to 12 at once (24 threads, 14.8 GB free)". Each open part's kernel is multi-threaded: Open CASCADE splits booleans (cuts, joins and the features built on them) and meshing over several threads, and faces and edges are read and boxed in parallel too. The first part you open gets all the processor threads but two (at most 22); each further part, assembly or drawing kernel gets half the threads beyond two, from 2 to 8. On a PC with 4 or 5 threads the first part gets all but one and the others one thread; with 2 or 3 threads the first part gets two (about 30 % quicker than one on two cores) and the others one. Parts full of cuts and large imports gain most: 16 test parts rebuild about three times faster than on one thread (on a PC held to 4 threads, 9.2 s instead of 16.3 s). The browser version at razorcad.com/app does the same in a current browser (the website serves it cross-origin isolated, which shared memory needs). The session log says which kernel started ("Geometry kernel ready: multi-threaded, 22 threads"). Cuts made together: a run of cut features (extrude and revolve cuts with a blind, mid-plane or through end, holes other than tapped ones, and patterns and mirrors of cuts) is made in one boolean instead of one after another, each on a body with more faces than the last. The cuts wait until a feature needs the body as it really is (a fillet, a hole ending on a face, anything that picks model geometry) or the rebuild ends. The Giant Golfball (178 dimples) rebuilds in 2.5 s instead of 4.7 s, with exactly the same result. Editing the last cut feature makes only its own cut again: the rest is remembered. Editing a feature meshes again only the faces and edges it changed, and a part reopened from the model cache picks up where it left off without being built again.

sections.title: Common problems
sections.text: Problem What to do --- --- A fillet or projected edge loses its edge after a big change Edges are found again by their geometry and the faces beside them (see References that follow edits). If one is still lost, Tools ▸ Fix References lists it: Edit to re-pick it, or Remove missing. A mate moved to the wrong face, or shows a red ! Mates find their faces again by geometry. A face that is gone is listed in Tools ▸ Fix Mates: edit the mate to pick it again. A sketch on a model face doesn't follow the face Sketches on faces are stored as fixed planes. Use a reference plane driven by an equation when that matters. Project Edges can't see a sketch It only sees visible sketches earlier in the history. Show the sketch first. An STL body can't be filleted STL bodies with thousands of faces can't be filleted or chamfered and don't offer pickable edges. A fillet won't blend across two touching bodies Combine the bodies first. Open fails with a file filter error Fixed in 0.9.0-beta. Update RazorCAD. Unsaved work after a crash Reopen the part and accept the auto-save recovery.

sections.title: Rebuilding the executable
sections.text: python -m pip install pywebview pyinstaller pillow build.bat build.bat bundles app/ (including the 23 MB OpenCascade WebAssembly kernel) and razorcad.py into RazorCAD.exe with PyInstaller. If RazorCAD is open, the running copy is renamed to RazorCAD.old.exe and the new build is used from the next launch. installer\build_installer.bat builds RazorCAD.exe and then RazorCAD-Setup.exe. Set the version in version.txt first.

build.bat

sections.title: Code signing
sections.text: Both builds sign RazorCAD.exe, the thumbnail DLL and the setup once a code-signing certificate is set up; until then they say "Not signed" and carry on. tools\sign.py --check shows how signing is set up. installer\SIGNING.md explains how to get a certificate and set it up (a certificate on a USB token or in Windows by its thumbprint, a .pfx file, or a cloud signing service).

sections.title: Regression tests
sections.text: python tests/run_tests.py This rebuilds the test parts in tests/parts with the real geometry kernel in headless Microsoft Edge. It compares every body's volume, area, faces and edges (and flat patterns) with tests/expected.json, and the drawings of six test parts with their stored line counts and sizes. It also runs checks done as a user does them: sketching, dimensioning and extruding, drawings, assemblies, mates, references, standard parts, collisions, assembly features, macros, accessibility and more. It needs Python's playwright package and exits with 1 on any difference. --update stores new expected results, --only runs some of them, and --make-parts makes the test parts again from tests/make_parts.js. On a PC with 12 or more processor threads the run is split over several pages side by side (--jobs N; --jobs 1 runs everything in one page): about 27 s instead of 65 s on 24 threads. See tests/README.md. Timings: every run's times are kept per machine in tests/perf-history.json (not in git). A test markedly slower than its usual time is listed under Performance; --perf lists every time and --perf-strict fails the run on a slowdown. On GitHub the tests run for every push and pull request (.github/workflows/tests.yml), split over 6 machines side by side (--shard I/N, shared out by the times in tests/test-weights.json): some 15 minutes.

sections.title: Releases
sections.text: Pushing a version tag (for example v0.14.0-beta, matching version.txt) runs .github/workflows/release.yml: the tests, then RazorCAD.exe and the setup are built and a draft release is made with the setup, its read-me, checksums and notes from CHANGELOG.md (tools/release_notes.py). A version that already has a release is left alone. See installer/RELEASING.md.

A version that already has a release is left alone. See installer/RELEASING.md.

sections.title: The geometry kernel builds
sections.text: app/vendor/replicad holds two builds of the same Open CASCADE bindings: replicad_single (one thread) and replicad_multi (threads, with shared memory). Both are built from source: Open CASCADE 8.0.1 with two speed patches (the same results), opencascade.js 3.1.0 (Emscripten 6.0.5) with whole-program optimisation, replicad's bindings (commit a0bc495) with RazorCAD's additions, and tools/native/surface-patch.cpp (tools/native/README.md); tools/patch_surface_kernel_loader.py adjusts their loaders. The kernel worker loads the multi-threaded one when the app asks for more than one thread and the page is cross-origin isolated: the desktop app's server, serve.py and the tests' server send Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp for that. The website takes files up to 25 MiB, so tools/build_web_app.py publishes a bigger kernel in parts, which the worker joins.

sections.title: The website and the browser version
sections.text: python tools/build_website_docs.py builds the online manual (website/docs) from this manual's source and the browser version (tools/build_web_app.py). The browser version is built in its own folder, RazorCAD Web next to the project folder, with both kernels (website/_headers serves it cross-origin isolated, so it runs the multi-threaded one where the browser can), and copied from there into website/app; it carries the geometry kernel's signature so the browser keeps stored models per kernel. python tools/check_site.py checks the website as it is served (razorcad.com, or another address): its pages, the browser version's isolation headers, and the browser version itself in headless Edge (it starts, and a multi-threaded kernel builds a part). GitHub runs it after each push that changes the website (.github/workflows/site-check.yml).

sections.title: Working on the UI
sections.text: Run python serve.py and open http://localhost:8765/ in a browser. In that mode files are downloaded instead of saved through dialogs. Set the RAZORCAD_DATA_DIR environment variable to keep a test run's recent-files list separate from your own.
